The X-ray Halo Scaling Relations of Supermassive Black Holes

M. Gaspari1,∗,†, D. Eckert2, S. Ettori3,4, P. Tozzi5, L. Bassini6,7, E. Rasia6,8, F. Brighenti9,

Abstract

We carry out a comprehensive Bayesian correlation analysis between hot halos and direct masses of supermassive black holes (SMBHs), by retrieving the X-ray plasma properties (temperature, luminosity, density, pressure, masses) over galactic to cluster scales for 85 diverse systems. We find new key scalings, with the tightest relation being the M∙−TxM_{\bullet}-T_{\rm x}, followed by M∙−LxM_{\bullet}-L_{\rm x}. The tighter scatter (down to 0.2 dex) and stronger correlation coefficient of all the X-ray halo scalings compared with the optical counterparts (as the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e}) suggest that plasma halos play a more central role than stars in tracing and growing SMBHs (especially those that are ultramassive). Moreover, M∙M_{\bullet} correlates better with the gas mass than dark matter mass. We show the important role of the environment, morphology, and relic galaxies/coronae, as well as the main departures from virialization/self-similarity via the optical/X-ray fundamental planes. We test the three major channels for SMBH growth: hot/Bondi-like models have inconsistent anti-correlation with X-ray halos and too low feeding; cosmological simulations find SMBH mergers as sub-dominant over most of the cosmic time and too rare to induce a central-limit-theorem effect; the scalings are consistent with chaotic cold accretion (CCA), the rain of matter condensing out of the turbulent X-ray halos that sustains a long-term self-regulated feedback loop. The new correlations are major observational constraints for models of SMBH feeding/feedback in galaxies, groups, and clusters (e.g., to test cosmological hydrodynamical simulations), and enable the study of SMBHs not only through X-rays, but also via the Sunyaev-Zel’dovich effect (Compton parameter), lensing (total masses), and cosmology (gas fractions).

Subject headings
SMBH/AGN feeding and feedback – hot halos (ICM, IGrM, CGM, ISM) – X-ray/optical observations: galaxies,  groups, clusters – hydrodynamical and cosmological simulations

I. Introduction

Supermassive black holes (SMBHs) are found at the center of most – if not all – galaxies (e.g., Kormendy & Ho 117 for a review). High-resolution observations of stellar and cold gas kinematics in the central regions of nearby galaxies have enabled dynamical measurements of central SMBH masses in over a hundred objects [132, 59, 82, 92, 14, 188, 250, e.g.,]. The measured masses of the SMBHs are correlated with the luminosity (LKL_{K}) and effective velocity dispersion (σe\sigma_{\rm e}) of the host galaxy, suggesting a co-evolution between the SMBH and the properties of their host environments. These findings further imply an interplay between the feeding/feedback mechanisms of the SMBH and its host galaxy [202]. During the active galactic nucleus (AGN) phase, outflows and jets from the central SMBH are thought to play a fundamental role in establishing the multiphase environment in their host halo, quenching cooling flows/star formation, and shaping the galaxy luminosity function [56, 218, 219, 143, 144, 114, 61, e.g.,]. For these reasons, AGN feedback has become a crucial ingredient in modern galaxy formation models [201, 25, 24, 73, 74, 245, 223, e.g.,].

While SMBH feedback is central to galaxy evolution, the mechanism through which the observed correlations between BH mass M∙M_{\bullet} and galaxy (or halo) properties are established is still debated. In the simple, idealized gravitational scenario, BH seeds are thought to grow rapidly at high redshift, with the scaling relations arising from the bottom-up structure formation process in which large structures are formed through the merging of smaller structures under the action of gravity (leading to virialization and self-similarity; e.g., Kravtsov & Borgani 118). In this scenario, the central SMBHs of the merging systems settle to the bottom of the potential well of the newly formed halo and eventually merge, inducing hierarchical scaling relations between M∙M_{\bullet} and galaxy properties (e.g., Peng 171, Jahnke & Macciò 106).

However, in recent years, measurements of BH masses in the most massive local galaxies (ultramassive black holes – UMBHs) have challenged the hierarchical formation scenario [137, 97, 98, 136, 217, e.g.,]. Some studies reported dynamical masses in excess of 1010​M⊙10^{10}M_{\odot}, i.e. about an order of magnitude greater than expected from the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} and M∙−LKM_{\bullet}-L_{K} relations. A prominent example of such an outlier is M87 (NGC 4486), for which the BH mass of 6.5×109​M⊙6.5\times 10^{9}M_{\odot} lies an order of magnitude above that expected from the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation [83]. Spectacular observations by the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) have recently confirmed the extreme mass of this object [54, 55]. Recent works have suggested that the environment and location of such UMBHs at the bottom of the potential well of galaxy clusters and groups, where the most massive galaxies are formed (known as brightest cluster/group galaxies – BCGs/BGGs), could be responsible for the observed deviations [71, 22, 11].

Beyond the stellar component, an important ingredient for SMBH feeding is the surrounding X-ray emitting plasma halo. At scales beyond the effective galactic radius, the majority of baryons are found in the form of a diffuse (ne<0.1​cm−3n_{\rm e}<0.1\;{\rm cm}^{-3}) and hot (Tx>0.1T_{\rm x}>0.1 keV) plasma, often referred to as the circumgalactic (CGM), intragroup (IGrM), or intracluster medium (ICM – e.g., Sarazin 191, Mathews & Brighenti 134, Kravtsov & Borgani 118, Sun 209, Gonzalez et al. 86, Eckert et al. 48). In the central regions of relaxed, cool-core (CC) systems, the plasma densities are such that the cooling time of the hot ICM/IGrM becomes much smaller than the Hubble time. Thus, a fraction of the hot gas11 1 For consistency with the literature, we refer interchangeably to the diffuse plasma component by using the ‘gas’ nomenclature. cools and condenses in the central galaxy, forming extended warm filaments detected in Hα\alpha and cold molecular clouds that fuel star formation (e.g., Fabian et al. 57, Peterson & Fabian 173, Combes et al. 37, McDonald et al. 139, McDonald et al. 140, McDonald et al. 142, Gaspari 70, Molendi et al. 152, Temi et al. 216, Tremblay et al. 220, Tremblay et al. 222, Nagai et al. 156). A portion of the cooling gas ignites the central AGN, which triggers the SMBH response via outflowing material that regulates the cooling flow of the macro-scale gaseous halo [19, 181, 143, 71, e.g.,]. Such SMBHs follow an intermittent duty cycle [20], as evidenced by the common presence of radio-emitting AGN, especially in massive galaxies [29, 150, 17, 133].

Over the past decade, extensive investigations have been carried out in order to understand the mechanism through which AGN inject energy into the surrounding medium and how the condensed filaments/clouds form out of the hot halos [72, 73, 74, 80, 176, 138, 199, 126, 178, 179, 234, 236, 228, 205, 246]. A novel paradigm has emerged in which the AGN feedback cycle operates through chaotic cold accretion (CCA; Gaspari et al. 77, Gaspari et al. 79, Gaspari et al. 80), where turbulent eddies induced by AGN outflows (and cosmic flows; Lau et al. 125) are responsible for the condensation of multiphase gas out of the hot halos via nonlinear thermal instability. The condensed gas then rapidly cools and rains toward the central SMBH. Within r<100r<100 pc, the clouds start to collide inelastically and get efficiently funneled inward within a few tens of Schwarzschild radii, where an accretion torus rapidly pushes the gas through the BH horizon via magneto-rotational instability (MRI; e.g., Balbus 8, Sa̧dowski & Gaspari 192). A growing body of studies suggests that, in spite of the mild average Eddington ratios22 2 The Eddington ratio is defined as follows: M˙Edd≡LEdd/(0.1​c2)≃22.8​(M∙/109​M⊙)​M⊙​yr−1\dot{M}_{\rm Edd}\equiv L_{\rm Edd}/(0.1\,c^{2})\simeq 22.8\,(M_{\bullet}/10^{9}\,M_{\odot})\,M_{\odot}\,{\rm yr^{-1}}, where LEdd=1047​(M∙/109​M⊙)​erg​s−1L_{\rm Edd}=10^{47}(M_{\bullet}/10^{9}\,M_{\odot})\;{\rm erg\,s^{-1}} is the Eddington luminosity., the mass accreted through CCA over long timescales can account for a substantial fraction of the SMBH masses (e.g., Gaspari et al. 77, Gaspari et al. 79, Voit et al. 235, Tremblay et al. 221, Tremblay et al. 222, Prasad et al. 179). Alternative models treat BH accretion purely from the single-phase, hot gas perspective, following the seminal work by Bondi [23] and related variants (e.g., Narayan & Fabian 159), predicting unintermittent accretion rates inversely tied to the plasma entropy. Further models, such as hierarchical major/minor mergers and high-redshift quasars, are tackled in §IV, in particular by means of cosmological simulations.

This work is part of the BlackHoleWeather program (PI: M. Gaspari), which aims at understanding the link between the central SMBH and its surrounding halo, both from the theoretical and observational points of view. Historically, this paper was initiated five years ago, inspired by the thorough review by Kormendy & Ho [117]. We make use of precise dynamical (direct) SMBH mass measurements collected from the literature [117, 136, 250] over a wide range of systems – including central galaxies and satellites, early- and late-type galaxies (ETGs, LTGs) – and correlate them with the properties of the surrounding hot X-ray atmosphere (X-ray luminosity, temperature, gas mass, pressure/thermal energy, and entropy). A tight correlation between M∙−TxM_{\bullet}-T_{\rm x} and M∙−LxM_{\bullet}-L_{\rm x} is indeed expected based on first-principle arguments initially proposed by Gaspari & Sa̧dowski [71]. We focus here only on hot X-ray plasma halos and related SMBHs, leaving halos falling below this band to future work (e.g., UV and related intermediate mass BHs – IMBHs). We further compare the X-ray scalings with the optical counterparts via both univariate and multivariate correlations. We discover new correlations between the various hot gas properties and SMBH mass, which help us to test the main models of macro-scale BH feeding, i.e., hot Bondi-like accretion, CCA, and hierarchical mergers. With the advent of gravitational-wave astronomy (LISA), direct SMBH imaging (EHT), and next-generation X-ray instruments with superb angular resolution and sensitivity (Athena, XRISM, and the proposed Lynx and AXIS), it is vital to understand how SMBHs form and grow.

This work is structured as follows. In §II, we present the retrieved data sample (85 galaxies) from a thorough literature search. In §III, we describe the main results in terms of a robust Bayesian statistical analysis of all the X-ray and optical properties (via univariate and multivariate correlations; Table 1). In §IV, we probe the main models of BH feeding and discuss key astrophysical insights arising from the presented correlations. In §V, we summarize the major results of the study and provide concluding remarks. As used in most literature studies, we adopt throughout the work a flat concordance cosmology with H0=70​km​s−1​Mpc−1H_{0}=70\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} (h=0.7h=0.7) and (Ωm,ΩΛ)=(0.3,0.7)(\Omega_{\rm m},\Omega_{\Lambda})=(0.3,0.7). The Hubble time is tH≡1/H0≃13.9t_{\rm H}\equiv 1/H_{0}\simeq 13.9 Gyr, which well approximates the age of the universe.

II. Data Analysis

II.1. Data sample and fundamental properties

The main objective of this study is to measure the observed correlations between direct SMBH masses and both the stellar and plasma halo properties. To achieve this goal, we performed a thorough search of the past two decades of the related observational literature aimed at assembling the fundamental observables in both the optical and X-ray band for a large sample of (85) galaxies. The selection is straightforward: we inspected any SMBH with a direct/dynamical BH mass measurement (van den Bosch 250) and looked for an available X-ray detection, in terms of galactic, group, and cluster emission from diffuse hot plasma. We tested combinations of these datasets, with comparable results. The potential role of selection effects is discussed in §IV.4. The retrieved, homogenized fundamental variables are listed in Appendix B, including the detailed references and notes for each galaxy in the sample. In the next two subsections, we describe their main optical and X-ray features.

II.1.1 Optical stellar observables and BH masses

Table 2 lists all the optical properties and BH masses of the galaxies in our sample. The vast majority of the BH masses come from van den Bosch [250], who compiled high-quality, dynamical measurements, mostly from Gültekin et al. [92], Sani et al. [190], Beifiori et al. [14], McConnell & Ma [136], Kormendy & Ho [117], Rusli et al. [186], and Saglia et al. [188]. Direct methods imply resolving the stellar or (ionized) gas kinematics shaped by the BH influence region G​M∙/σv2∼1GM_{\bullet}/\sigma_{v}^{2}\sim 1 -100 pc (for a few galaxies, water masers or reverberation mapping are other feasible methods; see Kormendy & Ho 117 for a technical review). Such scales require observations with arcsec/sub-arcsec resolution (the majority of which have been enabled by HST), thus limiting direct BH detections to the local universe (distance D<150D<150 Mpc or redshift z<0.04z<0.04).33 3 The evolution factor is negligible, given the low-redshift sample: E⁡(z)=Ωm​(1+z)3+ΩΛ<1.02E(z)=\sqrt{\Omega_{\rm m}(1+z)^{3}+\Omega_{\Lambda}}<1.02. One case (M87) includes the first direct imaging of the SMBH horizon available via EHT (Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration 54). In this study we focus on X-ray halos and related SMBHs, leaving BHs associated with gaseous halos emitting below the X-ray band to future investigations (i.e., IMBHs with M∙<∼3×107​M⊙M_{\bullet}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\displaystyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr<\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\textstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr<\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\scriptstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr<\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\scriptscriptstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr<\crcr\sim\crcr}}}}3\times 10^{7}\,M_{\odot}). Further, we do not include SMBH masses with major upper limits (e.g., NGC 4382, UGC 9799, NGC 3945) or which are substantially uncertain in the literature (e.g., Cygnus A, NGC 1275). The direct BHs with reliable X-ray data are listed, in ascending order, in column (vi) of Table 2, for a total robust sample of 85 BHs, spanning a wide range of masses M∙∼4×107M_{\bullet}\sim 4\times 10^{7} - 2×1010​M⊙2\times 10^{10}\,M_{\odot}. We remark that it is crucial to adopt direct BH mass measurements, instead of converting a posteriori from the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} and M∙−LKM_{\bullet}-L_{K} relations, or the AGN fundamental plane (Merloni et al. 147), which can lead to biased, non-independent correlations with unreliable conversion uncertainty >∼1\mathrel{\mathchoice{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\displaystyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr>\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\textstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr>\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\scriptstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr>\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\scriptscriptstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr>\crcr\sim\crcr}}}}1 dex (Fujita & Reiprich 64, Mittal et al. 150, Main et al. 133, Phipps et al. 175).

Unless noted in Table 2, the stellar velocity dispersion, effective radius, and total luminosity are from the collection by van den Bosch [250], who further expanded the optical investigations by Cappellari et al. [32], Kormendy & Ho [117], McConnell & Ma [136], and Saglia et al. [188]. All the collected properties are rescaled as per our adopted distances DD (column (v) in Tab. 2; e.g., M∙∝DM_{\bullet}\propto D and LK∝D2L_{K}\propto D^{2}). The measurement of the (effective) stellar velocity dispersion σe\sigma_{\rm e} is typically carried out via long-slit or integral-field-unit (IFU) spectroscopy, by measuring the optical emission-line broadening of the spectrum integrated within the effective half-light radius ReR_{\rm e} (or by the luminosity-weighted – LW – average of its radial profile; McConnell & Ma 136). Note that σe\sigma_{\rm e} is a one-dimensional (1D), line-of-sight velocity dispersion. An excellent proxy for the the total (bulge plus eventual disk) stellar luminosity is the near-infrared (NIR) luminosity in the KsK_{\rm s} band (rest-frame 2.0 - 2.3 μ\mum)44 4 We drop the ‘s’ (short) subscript throughout the manuscript, using only the KK band nomenclature., given its very low sensitivity to dust extinction (and star formation efficiencies). van den Bosch [250] carried out a detailed photometric growth-curve analysis based on a non-parametric determination of the galaxy LKL_{K} and half-light radii. This Monte-Carlo method fits each galaxy several hundred times with Sérsic profiles in which the outermost index is incrementally varied (0.5<n<40.5<n<4) until convergence is reached, thus leading to the listed total luminosity and effective radius ReR_{\rm e} (column (viii) and (x) in Tab. 2; the latter related to the major axis of the isophote containing 50% of the emitted NIR light). In our final sample, the range of stellar luminosities spans LK∼1010L_{K}\sim 10^{10} - 1012​L⊙10^{12}\,L_{\odot}, with effective radii between 1 - 100 kpc. Total luminosities can be further converted to stellar masses by using the mean stellar mass-to-light ratio (Kormendy & Ho 117):

log⁡M∗/LK=0.29​log⁡(σe/km​s−1)−0.64±0.09.\log M_{\ast}/L_{K}=0.29\log(\sigma_{\rm e}/{\rm km\,s^{-1}})-0.64\pm 0.09. (1)

About 1/3 of our galaxies have a significant disk component, which is reflected in a bulge-to-total luminosity ratio B/T<1B/T<1 (column (xi) in Tab. 2, from the photometric decomposition, mostly by Beifiori et al. 14, Kormendy & Ho 117, Saglia et al. 188). The collected B/TB/T, together with the above mass-to-light ratio, also allows us to compute the bulge mass MbulgeM_{\rm bulge}, in case they are not directly available (e.g., Beifiori et al. 14).

Besides the commonly adopted galaxy name (usually from NGC), Table 2 lists the PGC identification number (HyperLEDA), which is useful to track the position of the galaxy within the group/cluster halo (§II.1.2) and to identify the number of members NmN_{\rm m} in the large-scale, gravitationally bound cosmic structure. As shown in column (iv), NmN_{\rm m} covers values of 1 - 2 (isolated galaxies), 2 - 8 (fields), 8 - 50 (groups), and 50 - 1000 (clusters of galaxies). Because our search is carried out blindly in terms of the optical galactic properties, we have inherited a diverse mix of Hubble morphological types (Beifiori et al. 14, Kormendy & Ho 117, Saglia et al. 188), spanning from strong ETGs (E0-E4, including massive cD galaxies), to intermediate lenticulars S0s, and non-barred/barred spiral LTGs (see column (iii) in Tab. 2). Moreover, it is evident by visual inspection that late types/early types correlate with both low/high B/TB/T and NmN_{\rm m} values (poor/rich environments), as well as low/high BH masses. In all the subsequent correlation plots, LTGs, S0s, and ETGs are marked with cyan, green, and blue circles, respectively. However, unlike a few previous works, we do not attempt to divide a posteriori LTGs and ETGs in the Bayesian analysis in order to seek a smaller scatter, as we want to retain a sample that is as unbiased as possible.

II.1.2 X-ray plasma observables

Table 3 lists all the fundamental X-ray and environmental properties of the 85 galaxies, groups, and clusters in our sample, as well as related references and single-object notes. As introduced in §II.1.1, we carefully inspected the literature, choosing representative works with the deeper high-resolution Chandra and wide-field ROSAT/XMM-Newton datasets of hot halos (e.g., for the galactic scale, O’Sullivan et al. 162, Diehl & Statler 41, Nagino & Matsushita 157, Kim & Fabbiano 112, Su et al. 208, Goulding et al. 87, to name a few).

The first fundamental plasma observable is the X-ray luminosity, which is constrained from the X-ray photon flux (through either the count rate estimated in CCD images or the normalization of the energy spectra), Lx=fx​ 4​π​D2L_{\rm x}=f_{\rm x}\,4\pi D^{2}. Wherever necessary, given the cosmological distance dependence, luminosities (and radii) are rescaled via our adopted DD (or alternatively via our h=0.7h=0.7)55 5 Luminosities scale as ∝h−2\propto h^{-2} and radii as ∝h−1\propto h^{-1}.. Several of the above studies constrain LxL_{\rm x} within the (Chandra) X-ray broad band with rest-frame energy range 0.3​-​ 7​keV{\rm 0.3\,\text{-}\,7\;keV}, i.e., above the UV regime and including both soft and hard X-rays), making it our reference band too. For data points in a different X-ray energy range (e.g., in the soft66 6 It is interesting to note that, by using the soft X-ray band, one can better separate the diffuse gas component from that associated with contaminating AGN/shocks (which dominate in hard X-rays; e.g., LaMassa et al. 120). 0.5 - 2 keV band or pseudo-bolometric 0.05 - 50 keV) we apply the appropriate correction by using PIMMS77 7 http://cxc.harvard.edu/toolkit/pimms.jsp. tools. These corrections range between 5 - 30%. Further, the considered studies aim to remove the contaminations due to foreground/background AGN, low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) and fainter sources as active binaries/cataclysmic variables (ABs/CVs; see Goulding et al. 87), as well as correcting for Galactic neutral hydrogen absorption (log⁡NH/cm−2∼20\log N_{\rm H}/{\rm cm^{-2}}\sim 20 - 21). As for the optical morphological types, our final sample contains both gas-poor and gas-rich galaxies and groups/clusters (though only a handful of very massive clusters), spanning a wide range of (unabsorbed) luminosities Lx∼1038L_{\rm x}\sim 10^{38} - 104510^{45} erg s-1.

The second key observable of hot halos is the X-ray temperature, inferred from the detected energy spectrum (e.g., via ACIS-S or RGS instruments). Modern spectral codes with atomic lines libraries (including photoionization and recombination rates) are employed to achieve an accurate fitting, the majority using XSPEC with 1-TT (or seldom 2-TT) APEC models. A typical – though not unique – procedure among the collected studies of ETGs is as follows (e.g., Kim & Fabbiano 112). After removal of the X-ray point sources (including the central AGN, e.g., via CIAO wavedetect), the spectra are fitted with a multi-component model, including a thermal plasma APEC (diffuse plasma), hard X-ray power laws (residual AGN and AB/CV), and thermal 7 keV Bremsstrahlung (unresolved LMXBs). The assumed abundances (ranging between 0.3 - 1 Z⊙Z_{\odot}) are usually a source of significant uncertainty. The temperature (and emission measure) retrieved in varying annuli are then deprojected into a three-dimensional (3D) profile (e.g., via XSPEC projct). We remark that our focus is on the X-ray component related to the diffuse thermal gas. As tested by Goulding et al. [87], using alternative plasma models (e.g., MEKAL or variations in AtomDB) leads to TxT_{\rm x} variations of up to 10%; hence, on top of statistical errors, we conservatively add (in quadrature88 8 We checked that adding such errors in a linear way has a negligible impact on the correlation results, since systematic errors are ∼\sim 2×2\times larger than statistical errors. Further, given that all these errors are relatively small (in log space), using the sole statistical error induces only minor variations in the fit, with posterior parameters remaining comparable within the 1-σ\sigma fitting uncertainty.) a 10% systematic uncertainty to allow for a more homogeneous comparison. For analogous reason, we add a systematic error on LxL_{\rm x} by propagating the distance errors (10 - 20%). We note whenever archival errors are given in linear space, we transform and symmetrize them in logarithmic space. The final range of hot halo temperatures for our sample covers the entire X-ray regime, spanning Tx∼0.2T_{\rm x}\sim 0.2 - 8 keV.

The diffuse hot plasma can fill different regions of the potential well, including the galactic scale, the core and outskirt regions of the macro group/cluster halo. We thus use three main extraction regions as proxies for three characteristic X-ray radii within the potential well. The radius Rx,gR_{\rm x,g} is that describing the galactic/CGM potential. We thus searched for studies with LxL_{\rm x} and TxT_{\rm x} covering the region within ≈\approx 2​Re2R_{\rm e} (∼\sim 0.03 R500R_{500}; columns (iii-v) in Tab. 3), as X-ray halos are typically more diffuse than the stellar component. Beyond such radius, the background noise becomes significant for several of the isolated galaxies, and thus this radius defines a characteristic size within which most of the galactic X-ray halo is contained. Using the CGM region also helps to avoid inner, residual AGN contaminations. The second and third scales are related to Rx,c≈0.15​R500R_{\rm x,c}\approx 0.15\,R_{\rm 500} and 1​R5001\,R_{500}99 9 R500R_{500} is the radius that confines an average (total) matter density 500×500\times the critical cosmic density ρc\rho_{\rm c}, such that Mtot,500=(4/3)​π​ 500​ρc​R5003M_{\rm tot,500}=(4/3)\pi\,500\rho_{\rm c}R_{500}^{3}, where ρc=3​H2/(8​π​G)\rho_{\rm c}=3H^{2}/(8\pi G)., i.e., the core and outskirt radius of the group/cluster halo, respectively (columns (viii) and (x)). The latter is also a good proxy for the virial radius, R500≃Rvir/1.7R_{500}\simeq R_{\rm vir}/1.7, and is directly given by the X-ray temperature, R500≃860​kpc​(Tx,500/3​keV)1/2R_{500}\simeq{\rm 860\;kpc}\,(T_{\rm x,500}/{\rm 3\,keV})^{1/2} (0.03 dex scatter; Sun et al. 212).1010 10 Errors on Rx,gR_{\rm x,g} and Rx,cR_{\rm x,c} are given by the systematic error on distance plus a random error with 0.2 dex RMS; error on R500R_{500} is propagated from the Sun et al. [212] scaling. We note that non-BCGs/BGGs without a macro halo have core radius =0.15​R500=0.15\,R_{\rm 500}. To recap, our final collected archival sample has the following three mean (with RMS) extraction radii:

log⁡Rx,g\displaystyle\log R_{\rm x,g} =(0.22±0.33)+log⁡Re\displaystyle=(0.22\pm 0.33)+\log R_{\rm e}
=(−1.59±0.30)+log⁡R500\displaystyle=(-1.59\pm 0.30)+\log R_{500}
=(1.00±0.35)+log⁡kpc,\displaystyle=(1.00\pm 0.35)+\log{\rm kpc}, (2)
log⁡Rx,c\displaystyle\log R_{\rm x,c} =(1.00±0.28)+log⁡Re\displaystyle=(1.00\pm 0.28)+\log R_{\rm e}
=(−0.82±0.13)+log⁡R500\displaystyle=(-0.82\pm 0.13)+\log R_{500}
=(1.70±0.23)+log⁡kpc,\displaystyle=(1.70\pm 0.23)+\log{\rm kpc}, (3)
log⁡R500=(2.55±0.16)+log⁡kpc.\displaystyle\log R_{500}=(2.55\pm 0.16)+\log{\rm kpc}. (4)

The three extraction radii cover a healthy geometric progression of one-order-of-magnitude increments in spatial scale, ∼\sim 10−210^{-2} - 10−110^{-1} - 10010^{0} R500R_{500}. Note that in a literature search we can not control a sharp threshold, but only select approximate regions (Tab. 3). However, a sharp line in the sand is unphysical, since hot atmospheres are continuous in space. Having a dispersion on extraction radii also corroborates the robustness of any retrieved low intrinsic scatter.

To assess whether the galaxy is central, satellite, or isolated, we use the Tully [225] PGC1 catalog (and correlated NmN_{\rm m} in Tab. 2; in uncertain cases, we also inspected the X-ray halo peak). Whenever the considered system matches the brightest (PGC1) central galaxy of the cluster or group, we list it as BCG or BGG in column (ii) of Tab. 3; we then search in the cluster/group literature for X-ray data of the core luminosity/temperature (Lx,cL_{\rm x,c}/Tx,cT_{\rm x,c}; columns (vi-vii)) and global Lx,500L_{\rm x,500} (column (ix); e.g., Reiprich & Böhringer 184, Osmond & Ponman 165, Hudson et al. 102, Panagoulia et al. 166, O’Sullivan et al. 163, Babyk et al. 7). Given the declining emissivity profile toward the outskirts, Tx,cT_{\rm x,c} is comparable to Tx,500T_{\rm x,500} within typical uncertainty (Vikhlinin et al. 231). In the opposite regime, galaxies that are satellites (moving at hundreds km​s−1{\rm km\,s^{-1}} relative to the macro weather), isolated (N≤2N\leq 2) or brightest in a poor field (BFGs; both having rapidly dropping gas density beyond 2​Re2R_{\rm e}) can only feed from the local hot halo, hence we use as ‘macro’ X-ray properties (e.g., Lx,500L_{\rm x,500}) the CGM observables (this also avoids uncertain extrapolations).

The large majority of the listed TxT_{\rm x}/LxL_{\rm x} are retrieved via single-aperture X-ray spectroscopy/photometry. Whenever such values are not tabulated by the authors, we integrate the given luminosity/density profile (Eq. 9) or compute the LW temperature from its deprojected profile within our median Rx,gR_{\rm x,g} or Rx,cR_{\rm x,c} (avoiding extrapolations beyond constrained data points). The 14 systems retrieved via this method are listed in the Notes of Tab. 3 (e.g., Nagino & Matsushita 157).

Finally, as for the optical properties, we do not include galaxies with unconstrained or unavailable X-ray data on extended hot halos (e.g., NGC 4751, NGC 7457, NGC 4486A). Given the significant pile-up effects, we exclude objects that are heavily contaminated or show purely an X-ray AGN point source (often hosting nuclear fast outflows/winds), as several of the available Markarian galaxies (e.g., Tombesi et al. 218). We also exclude a few systems with X-ray emission completely swamped by the large-scale FRII-jet lobes or bubbles (Cygnus A, 3C66B/UGC 1841, NGC 193), thus preventing a reliable determination of the diffuse hot halo. Nevertheless, as discussed in §IV.4, we decided to include the vast majority of X-ray systems with robust hot halo constraints, regardless of the dynamical or evolutionary stage, thus considering quiescent, fossil, feedback- and merger-heated systems, as well as major outliers (e.g., NGC 1600).

II.2. Data fitting: Bayesian estimator

One of the major advancements in statistical astronomy of the last decade has been the leverage of Bayesian inference methods, which substantially depart from classical methods (such as the simple least-squares estimator). As we are here concerned purely with linear fitting (in log10\log_{10} space1111 11 Throughout the manuscript, we drop the ‘10’ subscript and use the formalism log10≡log\log_{10}\equiv\log.), we adopt the widely tested and robust formalism proposed by Kelly [109], which is coded into the (IDL1212 12 IDL linmix: https://idlastro.gsfc.nasa.gov/ftp/pro/math/linmix_err.pro; IDL mlinmix: https://idlastro.gsfc.nasa.gov/ftp/pro/math/mlinmix_err.pro. or Python1313 13 Python linmix: https://github.com/jmeyers314/linmix. ) procedures linmix and mlinmix – for univariate and multivariate fitting, respectively. A key reason to use the Bayesian formalism for linear regression is that the intrinsic scatter (ϵ\epsilon) is treated as a free parameter, together with the normalization/intercept (α\alpha) and slope (β\beta). At the same time, linmix/mlinmix accounts for measurement errors in both the dependent and independent variable/s. Compared with previous statistical methods, as the BCES estimator (Bivariate Correlated Errors and intrinsic Scatter; Akritas & Bershady 3), linmix is more robust and unbiased even for small samples and large uncertainties (e.g., Sereno 197).

Formally, the Bayesian linmix method has the objective to find the regression coefficients of the form (for univariate fitting)

Y=α+β​X+ϵ,Y=\alpha+\beta\,X+\epsilon, (5)

with the measured values x=X±σxx=X\pm\sigma_{x} and y=Y±σyy=Y\pm\sigma_{y}; while for our multivariate model

Y=α+β1​X1+β2​X2+ϵ,Y=\alpha+\beta_{1}\,X_{1}+\beta_{2}\,X_{2}+\epsilon, (6)

with the measured values x1=X1±σx1x_{1}=X_{1}\pm\sigma_{x_{1}}, x2=X2±σx2x_{2}=X_{2}\pm\sigma_{x_{2}}, and y=Y±σyy=Y\pm\sigma_{y}. The covariance terms in measurement errors are typically negligible (e.g., Saglia et al. 188). In this work, all the carried-out regressions are linear in logarithmic space (e.g., y=log⁡M∙±σlog⁡M∙y=\log M_{\bullet}\pm\sigma_{\log M_{\bullet}} and x=log⁡Tx±σlog⁡Txx=\log T_{\rm x}\pm\sigma_{\log T_{\rm x}}).

Procedurally, the linmix algorithm first approximates the independent variable distribution as a mixture of Gaussian distribution functions (three1414 14 We tested a larger number of initial Gaussians, finding no significant differences in the correlation results. is typically sufficient). The posterior probability distributions are then efficiently constrained through a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method known as Gibbs sampler1515 15 A minimum/maximum number of MCMC iterations set as 5000/100000 (with four chains) is sufficient in most cases to reach convergence.. We quote as best-fit parameters (in the top-left inset of each correlation plot; see Fig. 1) the averages of these distributions with 1-σ\sigma errors given by the related standard deviation. For the univariate fitting we use

α=α¯±σα[intercept],\displaystyle\alpha=\overline{\alpha}\pm\sigma_{\alpha}\hskip 38.98013pt{\rm[intercept]}, (7)
β=β¯±σβ[slope​on​X],\displaystyle\beta=\overline{\beta}\pm\sigma_{\beta}\hskip 39.83368pt{\rm[slope\ on}\ X],
ϵ=ϵ¯±σϵ[intrinsic​scatter],\displaystyle\epsilon=\overline{\epsilon}\pm\sigma_{\epsilon}\hskip 45.52458pt{\rm[intrinsic\ scatter]},
corr=corr¯±σc​[correlation​coefficient],\displaystyle{\rm corr}=\overline{\rm corr}\pm\sigma_{\rm c}\hskip 8.5359pt[{\rm correlation\ coefficient}],

while for the multivariate fitting we use

α=α¯±σα[intercept],\displaystyle\alpha=\overline{\alpha}\pm\sigma_{\alpha}\hskip 38.98013pt{\rm[intercept]}, (8)
β1,2=β¯1,2±σβ1,2​[slope​on​X1​and​X2],\displaystyle\beta_{1,2}=\overline{\beta}_{1,2}\pm\sigma_{\beta_{1,2}}\hskip 9.10509pt{\rm[slope\ on}\ X_{1}\ {\rm and}\ X_{2}{\rm],}
ϵ=ϵ¯±σϵ[intrinsic​scatter],\displaystyle\epsilon=\overline{\epsilon}\pm\sigma_{\epsilon}\hskip 45.52458pt{\rm[intrinsic\ scatter]},
pcorr1,2=pcorr¯1,2±σp1,2[partialcorrelationcoeff.],\displaystyle{\rm pcorr_{1,2}}=\overline{\rm pcorr}_{1,2}\pm\sigma_{\rm p_{1,2}}\hskip 5.69046pt[{\rm partial\ correlation\ coeff.}],

where it is important to note that in the multi-dimensional fitting the meaningful correlation coefficient is the partial (conditional) pcorr, i.e., we want to understand the correlation between YY and one of the independent variables given the second control variable.

Unlike the classic Pearson correlation analysis, the Bayesian inference gives us precise errors (and distributions) on the correlation coefficient, bounded between [−1,+1][-1,+1], which we can use to compare in a clear way the significance of multiple correlations. We quantify the strength of a positive correlation as follows: ‘very strong’ (corr>0.85{\rm corr}>0.85), ‘strong’ (0.7<corr<0.850.7<{\rm corr}<0.85), ‘mild’ (0.5<corr<0.70.5<{\rm corr}<0.7), ‘weak’ (0.3<corr<0.50.3<{\rm corr}<0.5), and ‘absent’ (0.0<corr<0.30.0<{\rm corr}<0.3). Anti-correlations have simply the sign (negative) reversed. We remark the importance of providing uncertainties for all the parameters. In §III, we will dissect three kinds of major correlations, the univariate fitting between two fundamental X-ray/optical variables (Eq. 5), the univariate fitting between composite variables (again via Eq. 5, which has minimal number of free parameters), and the multivariate fitting between the fundamental X-ray/optical observables (Eq. 6).

III. Results

We start the presentation of the results with the correlations of the fundamental X-ray/optical variables (§III.1), namely temperature/velocity dispersion and luminosities/masses. We then continue with the univariate correlations of the derived variables (such as gas density and pressure) and conclude the analysis with the higher-dimensional correlations (§III.3). A synoptic table with all the analyzed correlations is given in Table 1, which may be directly used in other studies. The reader can also find in the top-left inset of each correlation plot all the posterior regression coefficients (Eq. 5 - 6). Needless to say, correlation does not necessarily imply causation. On the other hand, the combination of a tight intrinsic scatter, large correlation coefficient, and non-zero slope, all with small statistical errors, accumulate evidence that some properties are more central than others in shaping the growth of SMBHs (and vice versa).

III.1. Univariate correlations: fundamental variables

III.1.1 X-ray temperature and luminosity

One of the most fundamental X-ray properties is the plasma temperature (§II.1.2), which is also a measure of the gravitational potential ϕ⁡(r)\phi(r). As the gas collapses in the potential wells of the dark matter halos during the formation of the galaxy, group, or cluster, the baryons thermalize (converting kinetic energy into thermal energy mainly via shock heating; Kravtsov & Borgani 118) and reach approximate virial equilibrium, kb​Tx∝ϕk_{\rm b}T_{\rm x}\propto\phi (§III.3.2).1616 16 As is customary, we use interchangeably the temperature in K and keV units (1 keV ≃1.16×107\simeq 1.16\times 10^{7} K), even though the latter technically has the dimensionality of energy. Unlike the X-ray luminosity depending on gas mass and thus experiencing evacuation (e.g., via feedback processes), the plasma TxT_{\rm x} remains fairly stable in space and time (e.g., Gaspari et al. 78). Typically, TxT_{\rm x} is constant within the galactic region and shows at best a factor of 2 variations up to the outer regions (Vikhlinin et al. 230, Diehl & Statler 41), mostly due to radiative cooling. Given that most of the photons come from the core region, the core temperature is a reasonable proxy for the global/virial temperature (Tx,c≈Tx,500T_{\rm x,c}\approx T_{\rm x,500}), within total uncertainties.

Figure 1 shows that the (LW) X-ray temperature within the galactic scale Rx,gR_{\rm x,g} (left; Eq.  2) or within the macro-scale group/cluster core Rx,cR_{\rm x,c} (right; Eq.  3) are very tightly correlated with the BH mass. The intrinsic scatter ∼\sim0.21 - 0.25 dex is the smallest found among all the studied correlations (1-σ\sigma level shown as a filled light red band), in particular compared with all the other optical/stellar properties (§III.1.2) – including the stellar velocity dispersion which has 0.1 dex larger scatter. This is a key result, given the large sample size and diversity of systems, spanning from massive clusters and groups to isolated S0s and spiral galaxies (top-right to bottom-left sectors, or blue to green and cyan color-coding). The best-fit slopes are both consistent with a power-law index of 2.1 - 2.7, with correlation coefficients in the very strong regime (0.93 - 0.94). In terms of normalization, a 0.8 keV halo corresponds to a ∼\sim109​M⊙10^{9}\,M_{\odot} SMBH.

We will dissect in §IV what is the role of the potential versus different accretion mechanisms arising from the hot plasma halo. For now, it is worthwhile to understand the notion that a hotter halo leads to substantially more massive black holes (M∙∝Tx2.5M_{\bullet}\propto T_{\rm x}^{2.5}), up to even UMBHs in BCGs. This means that the accretion process shall be stimulated by the presence of a larger plasma mass (e.g., in galactic coronae or the more extended IGrM/ICM), rather than hindered by its thermal pressure, which tends to oppose the gas gravitational infall. The high end of the M∙−Tx,cM_{\bullet}-T_{\rm x,c} hints at a potential saturation, although at present it is unclear whether UMBHs with several tens of billions of solar masses exist in the universe.

Figure 2 shows the second fundamental X-ray variable, i.e., the plasma luminosity, enclosed within our three radial regions (top to bottom panel: Rx,gR_{\rm x,g}, Rx,cR_{\rm x,c}, and R500R_{500}, respectively; Eq. 2 - 4). As for the X-ray temperature, LxL_{\rm x} shows a very strong positive correlation with the black hole mass (corr >0.85>0.85). Regarding normalization, a typical SMBH of 109​M⊙10^{9}\,M_{\odot} tends to reside in a plasma halo of ∼\sim 1041​erg​s−110^{41}\,{\rm erg\,s^{-1}}. The log slope is now below unity, ranging between 0.5 - 0.4, adopting the galactic or cluster/virial scale, respectively (as LxL_{\rm x} steadily increases with radius). However, the range covered by LxL_{\rm x} is now over 6 dex, i.e., a 6×6\times range increase compared with the temperature log scaling (we checked that the Lx−TxL_{\rm x}-T_{\rm x} relation is consistent with that in other observational works which include low-mass galaxies; see §III.3.2 and Fig. 24). It is a major result that the SMBH scaling holds over such a wide range of X-ray luminosities, reflecting very different (poor and rich) environments. We note the R500R_{500} scalings are the more uncertain correlations: their contained scatter might be a reflection of the currently low number of available central massive galaxies (i.e., those having macro properties, such as Lx,500L_{\rm x,500}, set by the extended ICM and not the CGM; §II.1.2).

Another important difference with TxT_{\rm x} is the relatively larger intrinsic scatter in M∙−LxM_{\bullet}-L_{\rm x}, hovering in the range 0.29 - 0.31 dex, though still tighter than any optical scaling relation (Fig. 3). Removing the 3.5-σ\sigma outlier NGC 1600 (which could have stochastically suffered a ram-pressure halo stripping or AGN outburst) would reduce the scatter by 0.03 dex, approaching that of the temperature scalings. Conversely, a case of perfectly matching the mean best fit is provided by M87 (Lx,c≃1.2×1043​erg​s−1L_{\rm x,c}\simeq 1.2\times 10^{43}\;{\rm erg\,s^{-1}}), whose SMBH horizon has been recently imaged via EHT, constraining log⁡M∙/M⊙≃9.8\log M_{\bullet}/M_{\odot}\simeq 9.8. Interestingly, the lowest scatter in LxL_{\rm x} is found within the core region (though with small significance), where radiative cooling is very effective. Since Lx∝Mgas2​(<CLOSEL_{\rm x}\propto M^{2}_{\rm gas}(<\,OPENr)r), any gas evacuation (or phase transition) is associated with significant luminosity variations; indeed, feedback processes and mergers/cosmic inflows are particularly impactful in the inner and outer regions (e.g., Ghirardini et al. 84), respectively, while the intermediate region is less affected by them (the M∙−fgas,cM_{\bullet}-f_{\rm gas,c} relation will unveil this more clearly; §III.2.6). In §IV.1.2, we will test the role of gas condensation and CCA-regulated AGN feedback; indeed, the existence of a tight correlation between BH mass and LxL_{\rm x}/TxT_{\rm x} is consistent with first-principle predictions (Gaspari & Sa̧dowski 71).

We note that more massive SMBHs are hosted by galaxies with more extended X-ray and effective radii (e.g., M∙−Rx,gM_{\bullet}-R_{\rm x,g} has a mild correlation with slope 1.1±0.21.1\pm 0.2), as more luminous halos have larger atmospheres (Fig. 24). A stronger correlation emerges considering M∙−Rx,cM_{\bullet}-R_{\rm x,c} (β=2.4±0.3\beta=2.4\pm 0.3), although the BH correlations with characteristic radii typically show a significant scatter (∼\sim 0.4 dex; e.g., Fig. 14). The correlation with R500R_{500} is tighter and steeper, being a pure reflection of the TxT_{\rm x} scaling. The multivariate, partial correlation analysis in §III.3 combining all the fundamental observables will help to understand any potential X-ray virial relations or deviations from it via non-gravitational processes.

While finishing our five-year project, another short work discussed a correlation between M∙M_{\bullet} and cluster halo temperature in 17 BCGs/BGGs (Bogdán et al. 22; no X-ray value was used here from their paper). They find a best-fit log⁡(M∙/109​M⊙)=(0.20±0.09)+(1.74±0.16)​log⁡(Tx,c/keV)\log(M_{\bullet}/10^{9}\,M_{\odot})=(0.20\pm 0.09)+(1.74\pm 0.16)\log(T_{\rm x,c}/{\rm keV}) (with Tx,cT_{\rm x,c} as proxy for Tx,500T_{\rm x,500}). The shallower slope is due to a massive-system bias: selecting only central galaxies in our sample leads to log⁡(M∙/109​M⊙)=(0.20±0.07)+(1.83±0.31)​log⁡(Tx,c/keV)\log(M_{\bullet}/10^{9}\,M_{\odot})=(0.20\pm 0.07)+(1.83\pm 0.31)\log(T_{\rm x,c}/{\rm keV}), which is consistent with the above. Given their smaller sample and less robust BCES method (§II.2), their scatter is ∼\sim 0.1 dex higher, though still tighter than that of their M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e}. This marks the importance of collecting a larger and more complete sample covering different morphological, dynamical, and environmental types.

III.1.2 Optical/stellar velocity dispersion, luminosity, and bulge mass

We focus now on the counterpart variables in the optical band that are tracing the stellar component, rather than the plasma halo. Given that most stars are confined within a few effective radii, the optical properties can only trace the galactic scale, and not the larger scale core or virial region.

Fig. 3 shows the SMBH mass as a function of the three fundamental variables adopted in several previous studies: the 1D velocity dispersion σe\sigma_{\rm e} (within an aperture the size of effective radius ReR_{\rm e}), bulge mass, and total (bulge plus disk) galactic luminosity in the NIR (∼\sim 2.2​μ2.2\,\mum) KK band (§II). The first key result is the substantially larger intrinsic scatter of all the optical properties compared with that of the X-ray counterparts (Fig. 1 - 2), which can reach values up to 0.5 dex for LKL_{K}, with the correlation coefficient dropping to the mild (∼\sim 0.7) level.

The most reliable optical property is the stellar velocity dispersion σe\sigma_{\rm e} (top panel), which represents another tracer of the (inner) galactic potential σe2∝ϕg\sigma_{\rm e}^{2}\propto\phi_{\rm g} (§III.3.1). The retrieved σe\sigma_{\rm e} scatter is 0.36 dex, which is 0.15 - 0.11 dex larger than that of the galactic/core X-ray temperature (at over 99.9% confidence). The M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} log slope is 4.4±0.44.4\pm 0.4, which is consistent with twice that of the M∙−TxM_{\bullet}-T_{\rm x} scaling, i.e., σe2∝Tx\sigma_{\rm e}^{2}\propto T_{\rm x}, as expected in virialized systems1717 17 Specifically, σe2=kb​Tx/μ​mp\sigma_{\rm e}^{2}=k_{\rm b}T_{\rm x}/{\mu m_{\rm p}} (with μ=0.62\mu=0.62 the plasma particle mean weight); while we find a unity slope (0.93±0.080.93\pm 0.08) for σe2−Tx,g\sigma_{\rm e}^{2}-T_{\rm x,g}, the normalization is lower than the virial expectation by ≈\approx 40%, implying extra heating due to feedback processes.. The retrieved M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} slope is similar to that found by previous studies on bulge-dominated galaxies (e.g., Kormendy & Ho 117); it would steepen to a value >∼5\mathrel{\mathchoice{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\displaystyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr>\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\textstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr>\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\scriptstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr>\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\scriptscriptstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr>\crcr\sim\crcr}}}}5, almost doubling the intrinsic scatter, including the more uncertain low-mass BHs and related irregular galaxies (e.g., Saglia et al. 188). The high-mass end of the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} is a significant source of scatter with increasingly over-massive BHs (five objects are approaching the top 3-σ\sigma channel), in conjunction with the increased presence of BGGs/BCGs (see also Fig. 21; some works interpret this as a nonlinear bend). The disky (low B/TB/T) and spiral galaxies (green/cyan points) start also to show symptoms of a decline below the linear fit (despite measurements of σe\sigma_{\rm e} remaining accurate), while M∙−TxM_{\bullet}-T_{\rm x} and M∙−LxM_{\bullet}-L_{\rm x} retain a stable linear behavior regardless of different morphological types and environment (Fig. 21).

The second panel in Fig. 3 shows the M∙−LKM_{\bullet}-L_{K} scaling. While the total galaxy NIR luminosity is a good proxy for the total stellar mass (since it is not much affected by dust absorption), the hosted BH mass is only mildly tied to this galactic observable. Unlike the other quantities, the morphological types tend to be significantly mixed from low to large LKL_{K} values, corroborating the large ϵ\epsilon value. On the other hand, the slope is consistent with unity, i.e., there is a direct 1:1 conversion in both logarithmic and linear space, with an average 1011​L⊙10^{11}\,L_{\odot} galaxy hosting a M∙≃2×108​M⊙M_{\bullet}\simeq 2\times 10^{8}\,M_{\odot}. Converting LKL_{K} to total stellar mass (Eq. 1) would show similar correlation slope and scatter, within the 1-σ\sigma uncertainty (the total stellar mass correlations are thus redundant and not shown). At variance with temperatures, the X-ray versus optical luminosities (at all radii) show very different scaling with M∙M_{\bullet}, since LxL_{\rm x} covers four more orders of magnitude compared with LKL_{K}. In other words, the X-ray properties allow us to probe more extended regimes and regions than those traced by stars, better separating the loci occupied by LTGs and ETGs. The multivariate analysis (§III.3) will unveil that the X-ray and optical fundamental planes behave differently due to LxL_{\rm x} breaking the self-similar gravitational collapse expectation.

A way to reduce the scatter is to consider purely the stellar bulge mass, instead of the total stellar luminosity/mass (which is contaminated by potential disk features). The bottom panel in Fig. 3 shows the correlation with the stellar bulge mass (known as the ‘Magorrian relation’; Magorrian et al. 132). Translating from a luminosity to a mass is non-trivial since the M∗/LKM_{\ast}/L_{K} depends on complex stellar population models (§II.1). Moreover, the B/TB/T ratio should be taken as approximate, as it can vary significantly between studies. Keeping in mind such hurdles, the M∙−MbulgeM_{\bullet}-M_{\rm bulge} relation is able to reduce the scatter to 0.40 dex, albeit not yet reaching the lower level of σe\sigma_{\rm e}. The log slope is slightly shallower than unity (β≈0.9\beta\approx 0.9). Regarding normalization, Mbulge/M∙≈360M_{\rm bulge}/M_{\bullet}\approx 360, implying that stars continuously accumulate within the galaxy without substantially feeding the BH during cosmic time, given their collisionless nature.

The M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} appears to be the most stable optical estimator of BH mass. However, it presents signs of unreliability at the high-mass end, with several galaxies exceeding the 2-σ\sigma scatter band. None of the optical variables shows better correlations than the X-ray counterparts, in terms of intrinsic scatter and correlation coefficient (>> 9999% confidence level). Moreover, performing a pairwise correlation analysis on residuals (cf. Shankar et al. 198), we find that log⁡M∙−⟨log⁡M∙|log⁡σe⟩\log M_{\bullet}-\langle\log M_{\bullet}|\log\sigma_{\rm e}\rangle versus log⁡Tx−⟨log⁡Tx|log⁡σe⟩\log T_{\rm x}-\langle\log T_{\rm x}|\log\sigma_{\rm e}\rangle has 60% larger correlation coefficient (0.8) than log⁡M∙−⟨log⁡M∙|log⁡Tx⟩\log M_{\bullet}-\langle\log M_{\bullet}|\log T_{\rm x}\rangle versus log⁡σe−⟨log⁡σe|log⁡Tx⟩\log\sigma_{\rm e}-\langle\log\sigma_{\rm e}|\log T_{\rm x}\rangle, suggesting that X-ray properties are more fundamental than optical properties. There are two reasons that we deem to be important to explain this. First, the stellar component is tracing purely the inner part of the whole gravitational potential, thus missing the macro group/cluster halo. Second, stars are the residual by-product of a more wide-spread top-down multiphase condensation process, which originates in the X-ray plasma atmosphere (particularly in the core, r<∼0.1​R500r\mathrel{\mathchoice{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\displaystyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr<\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\textstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr<\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\scriptstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr<\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\scriptscriptstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr<\crcr\sim\crcr}}}}0.1\,R_{500}; §IV).

III.2. Univariate correlations: composite X-ray variables

We now move on to the univariate correlations of the composite variables, again focusing on their interplay with BH mass. Indeed, the equations of thermodynamics and hydrodynamics for a diffuse gas/plasma are linked to properties such as pressure and particle number density. The concept to keep in mind is to derive these properties only from the fundamental observables, i.e., X-ray luminosity and temperature (while propagating the related errors), thus keeping any parameterization and assumption to the minimum.

III.2.1 Electron number density

The plasma luminosity is given by

Lx=∫ne​ni​Λ​(Tx,Z)​𝑑V,L_{\rm x}=\int{n_{\rm e}n_{\rm i}\,\Lambda(T_{\rm x},Z)\,dV}, (9)

where Λ⁡(Tx,Z)\Lambda(T_{\rm x},Z) is the radiative plasma cooling function in collisional ionization equilibrium (Sutherland & Dopita 214)1818 18 The cooling curve includes spectral calculations for H, He, C, N, O, Fe, Ne, Na, Si, Mg, Al, Ar, S, Cl, Ca, Ni, and all related stages of ionization. We tested different cooling curves (e.g., Schure et al. 194), finding comparable results. adopting metallicity Z≃0.7, 0.4, 0.3​Z⊙Z\simeq 0.7,\,0.4,\,0.3\;Z_{\odot} for the galactic, core, and R500R_{500} region, respectively (Mernier et al. 149)1919 19 We tested the full observational scatter of observed abundance values, finding no major change in results. Further, we note that such changes in metallicity alter μi\mu_{\rm i} by less than 1%.. By differentiating and discretizing Eq. 9 over finite spherical shells, Δ​V=(4/3)​π​(Rout3−Rin3CLOSE\Delta V=(4/3)\pi(R_{\rm out}^{3}-R_{\rm in}^{3}), the plasma electron number density can be retrieved as

ne≃(Δ​LxΔ​V​μi/μeΛ⁡(Tx,Z))1/2,n_{\rm e}\simeq\left(\frac{\Delta L_{\rm x}}{\Delta V}\frac{{\mu_{\rm i}}/{\mu_{\rm e}}}{\Lambda(T_{\rm x},Z)}\right)^{1/2}, (10)

where (μi,μe)≃(1.30,1.18)(\mu_{\rm i},\mu_{\rm e})\simeq(1.30,1.18) are the ion and electron mean weights (for a plasma with solar composition). Given finite discretization of Eq. 9, the computed nen_{\rm e} should be understood as a mean density inside our three radial shells (0−-Rx,gR_{\rm x,g}, Rx,gR_{\rm x,g}−-Rx,cR_{\rm x,c}, Rx,cR_{\rm x,c}−-R500R_{500}).2020 20 For non-central galaxies, the core/outskirt gradients are approximated as d​Lx/d​V∼Lx/VdL_{\rm x}/dV\sim L_{\rm x}/V. Over our entire sample and bins, we find a median density gradient d​log⁡ne/d​log⁡r=−1.6±0.3d\log n_{\rm e}/d\log r=-1.6\pm 0.3, which is consistent with that in other works (e.g., Babyk et al. 7 and Hogan et al. 99). We remark that gas density is a composite variable given by the combination of X-ray luminosity, temperature, and Rx3R_{\rm x}^{3} (Eq. 10).

Figure 4 shows the correlation between SMBH mass and plasma electron density, inside our three adopted radial shells. For the inner scale the correlation is weak (absent at the 2-σ\sigma level), corroborated by the substantial scatter (ϵ≃0.6\epsilon\simeq 0.6) and the large errors in the posterior distributions (broad red bands). Indeed, most of the galaxies have an average galactic/CGM gas number density ranging between ne,g∼10−3n_{\rm e,g}\sim 10^{-3} - 10−210^{-2} cm-3 (consistently with other studies, e.g., Lakhchaura et al. 122). The correlation enters instead the strong regime (almost halving the scatter) if we consider the core or R500R_{500} region. This corroborates the result highlighted by the M∙−Lx,cM_{\bullet}-L_{\rm x,c} (§III.1.1), i.e., the halo core region (where the cooling time is typically below the Hubble time) is one of the best predictors for the SMBH growth. The slope is consistent with unity, with a typical SMBH mass of a few 109​M⊙10^{9}M_{\odot} (massive galaxies) linked to ne≈10−3/10−4n_{\rm e}\approx 10^{-3}/10^{-4} cm-3 in the macro-scale core/outskirt region (in agreement with values retrieved by Sun 209 and Hogan et al. 99 for BGGs and BCGs). Since LxL_{\rm x} (via ne2​Λn_{\rm e}^{2}\,\Lambda) is a direct manifestation of the plasma radiative emission, these findings suggest that condensation processes could play a major role in the evolution of SMBHs (§IV.1.2).

III.2.2 Total gas pressure

A key thermodynamic variable which determines the hydrostatic balance of a stratified atmosphere is the total gas/plasma pressure (P=Pe+PiP=P_{\rm e}+P_{\rm i}) defined as

P=n​kb​Tx,P=n\,k_{\rm b}T_{\rm x}, (11)

where n=ne+ni≃2​nen=n_{\rm e}+n_{\rm i}\simeq 2\,n_{\rm e} is the total gas particle number density. Figure 5 shows the M∙−PxM_{\bullet}-P_{\rm x} correlation for our three radial shells (§III.2.1). All the gas pressure scalings reside in the regime of strong correlation with BH mass (corr ≈0.7\approx 0.7 - 0.90.9). The direct combination of density and temperature seems to ameliorate the galactic scaling, although the scatter remains large at 0.5 dex. The best-fit slope is stable at sublinear values, β≈0.75\beta\approx 0.75. As for LxL_{\rm x}, the core region displays the lowest scatter (ϵ≃0.3\epsilon\simeq 0.3) and highest corr coefficient, with a characteristic gas pressure of ∼\sim 10−310^{-3} keV cm-3 for halos hosting a 109​M⊙10^{9}\,M_{\odot} BH.

Interestingly, more pressure-supported halos harbor larger SMBHs. If we think in terms of classical hot-mode accretion (Bondi, ADAF, etc.), in which a larger atmospheric pressure suppresses accretion (§IV.1.1), such a trend seems difficult to develop. However, if accretion proceeds through the cold mode, then a more pressurized gas implies larger available internal energy, P/(γ−1)P/(\gamma-1),2121 21 The (non-relativistic) plasma adiabatic index is γ=5/3\gamma=5/3. to be radiated away, and thus a larger condensing neutral/molecular gas mass available to rain onto the SMBH (dropping out of the diffuse atmosphere in quasi hydrostatic equilibrium).

III.2.3 Gas Mass

The plasma mass within a given enclosed radius can be retrieved (integrating over our bins) via

Mgas(<r′)=∫0r′ρ​ 4​π​r2​𝑑r,M_{\rm gas}(<r^{\prime})=\int^{r^{\prime}}_{0}\rho\;4\pi r^{2}dr, (12)

where the total gas density is ρ=ne​μe​mp=n​μ​mp\rho=n_{\rm e}\mu_{\rm e}m_{\rm p}=n\mu m_{\rm p}. Figure 6 shows the M∙−MgasM_{\bullet}-M_{\rm gas} correlations. In spite of being (here) a derived variable, MgasM_{\rm gas} is very well correlated with the BH mass, lowering the intrinsic scatter to ϵ≃0.26±0.03\epsilon\simeq 0.26\pm 0.03, comparable to that of the fundamental X-ray temperature scalings. Being an integrated quantity, gas mass has a smoothening advantage compared with local properties. In the core region (middle panel), the Bayesian posterior of the corr coefficient shows a value 0.92±0.030.92\pm 0.03, which is consistent with a maximal positive correlation at the 3-σ\sigma level. Evidently, the gas mass plays a key role in the evolution of SMBHs. The slope is similar across all radial bins, with values β≈0.6\beta\approx 0.6. The galactic (top panel) and virial (bottom panel) relations bound the locus of optimal correlation.

Regarding normalization, the median 109​M⊙10^{9}\,M_{\odot} BHs occupy core halos that have ∼\sim10×\times more gas mass. As a ratio, this is over an order of magnitude lower compared with that involving the stellar bulge mass (the Magorrian relation; §III.1.2). We note that the retrieved range of core gas masses Mgas,c∼109−1011​M⊙M_{\rm gas,c}\sim 10^{9}-10^{11}\,M_{\odot} is consistent with that of similar samples (e.g., Babyk et al. 7), corroborating our derivation method. Considering the galactic scale (top panel), the median SMBH has MgasM_{\rm gas} roughly equivalent to M∙M_{\bullet} (at least at z∼0z\sim 0). This suggests that, while a major fraction of the BH mass can be built up in time via gas accretion due to collisional processes (e.g., CCA inelastic collisions, hydrodynamical instabilities, viscosity, shocks, turbulent mixing), stars remain largely unaffected by the accretion process being collisionless systems. This may also explain why most stellar properties present substantial scatter as estimators of M∙M_{\bullet}, being linked to the BH growth via secondary/indirect effects.

III.2.4 YxY_{\rm x} Compton parameter – Thermal energy

Another key quantity that has become central to cluster and cosmological studies is the X-ray analog of the Compton YszY_{\rm sz} parameter (Kravtsov et al. 119), which describes the strength of the thermal Sunyaev-Zel’dovich (SZ) effect2222 22 The distortion of the cosmic microwave background spectrum via inverse Compton scattering by the hot plasma electrons (e.g., Khatri & Gaspari 110).. We define this X-ray analog as follows:

Yx≡Eth=32​kb​Txμ​mp​Mgas.Y_{\rm x}\equiv E_{\rm th}=\frac{3}{2}\frac{k_{\rm b}T_{\rm x}}{\mu m_{\rm p}}M_{\rm gas}. (13)

Multiplying by the relevant thermodynamic constants, YxY_{\rm x} represents another form of the plasma thermal energy content (or integrated pressure). Recent studies (e.g., Planelles et al. 177 and refs. within) agree that Yx,500Y_{\rm x,500} is a good proxy for the total mass, being relatively insensitive to feedback processes (e.g., the diffuse atmosphere is heated while being evacuated at the same time).

Figure 7 shows the M∙−YxM_{\bullet}-Y_{\rm x} relation within our three X-ray radii. The Compton parameter correlation is able to reduce the scatter compared with the linked (punctual) M∙−PxM_{\bullet}-P_{\rm x}: the galactic scaling indeed reduces the scatter down by 30%, which is near ϵ≃0.30\epsilon\simeq 0.30 across all regions. This is analogous to that of the gas mass scalings, except for the core region. The correlation coefficient remains in the very strong regime (corr≈0.9{\rm corr}\approx 0.9). The slope is shallow, down to a value of ∼\sim1/2; indeed, thermal energy covers a wide range of values from small spirals to massive BCGs, Eth,c≈1056E_{\rm th,c}\approx 10^{56} - 106210^{62} erg.

Interestingly, an SMBH of 109​M⊙10^{9}\,M_{\odot} has an available rest-mass feedback energy of E∙=η​M∙​c2∼2×1060E_{\bullet}=\eta\,M_{\bullet}c^{2}\sim 2\times 10^{60} erg (using a median mechanical efficiency η∼10−3\eta\sim 10^{-3}; Gaspari & Sa̧dowski 71) which can potentially unbind the galactic/core region if released in short time. However, such ejective (quasar-like) feedback matching the gas gravitational binding (∼\sim Mgas​ϕ≃2​EthM_{\rm gas}\phi\simeq 2E_{\rm th}) energy would induce M∙∼2​Yx/(η​c2)∝Mgas​σe2M_{\bullet}\sim{2\,Y_{\rm x}}/(\eta c^{2})\propto M_{\rm gas}\sigma_{\rm e}^{2} (the latter via σe2∝Tx\sigma_{\rm e}^{2}\propto T_{\rm x}; §III.1.2), leading to much steeper scaling than that found in Fig. 7 or 3. Thereby a gentler AGN feeding/feedback self-regulation and gradual deposition is required (§IV; see also Gaspari et al. 78).

Overall, the stability and tightness across largely different radial regions (varying each by one order of magnitude; §II.1.2) corroborates the importance of using YxY_{\rm x} over other thermodynamic observables (such as pressure or entropy). Such strong and tight correlations with the Compton parameter, particularly for the large-scale R500R_{500} region, imply that we can use the thermal SZ signal from hot halos to probe or trace SMBHs. This novel approach presents several advantages over the X-ray counterpart, since we can fully leverage the new ground-based radio facilities (instead of the more expensive X-ray space telescopes), which have recently entered a golden age (e.g., ALMA, MUSTANG-2, NIKA-2, SPT).

III.2.5 Total mass (dark matter, gas, stars)

We analyze now the total (gravitational) mass, which is the sum of the baryonic (gas and stars) and dark matter (DM) component. The latter dominates (>> 90%) the total matter content, particularly in the core and outskirt regions of the group/cluster. Studies show that the dark matter distribution can be well described by a NFW profile (Navarro et al. 160) in most galaxies and clusters (e.g., Humphrey et al. 103, Ettori et al. 52), which is shaped by one minimal parameter. While the global mass is given via R500R_{500} (§II.1.2), Mtot,500=(4/3)​π​R5003​ 500​ρcM_{\rm tot,500}=(4/3)\pi R_{500}^{3}\,500\rho_{\rm c}, the dark matter mass enclosed within smaller radii can be retrieved via the NFW profile

MDM(<r)=4​π​ρs​Rs3​[ln⁡(Rs+rRs)−rRs+r],M_{\rm DM}(<r)=4\pi\rho_{\rm s}\,R^{3}_{\rm s}\left[\ln{\left(\frac{R_{\rm s}+r}{R_{\rm s}}\right)}-\frac{r}{R_{\rm s}+r}\right], (14)

where the scale radius is Rs≡R500/c500R_{\rm s}\equiv R_{500}/c_{500} and the concentration parameter is given by observations of galaxies and groups (Sun et al. 212), c500≃5.0​(Mtot,500/1013​M⊙)−0.09c_{500}\simeq 5.0\left({M_{\rm tot,500}}/{10^{13}\,M_{\odot}}\right)^{-0.09} (with 0.1 dex scatter). The characteristic DM density is defined as

ρs=500​ρc3​c5003ln⁡(1+c500)−c500/(1+c500).\rho_{\rm s}=\frac{500\rho_{\rm c}}{3}\frac{c_{500}^{3}}{\ln(1+c_{500})-c_{500}/(1+c_{500})}. (15)

As secondary components of the total matter content, we add the enclosed gas mass (§III.2.3) and galaxy stellar mass (§III.1.2)2323 23 Albeit having minor role, we adopt a stellar (Hernquist 94) profile M∗(<r)=M∗,tot​[r2/(r+a)2]M_{\ast}(<r)=M_{\ast,\rm tot}\,[r^{2}/(r+a)^{2}], where a=Re/(1+2)a=R_{\rm e}/(1+\sqrt{2}). to the above DM mass. The retrieved total masses within R500R_{500} span a range of Mtot,500∼1012M_{\rm tot,500}\sim 10^{12} - 1015​M⊙10^{15}\,M_{\odot} from isolated galaxies to massive clusters (consistently with Forbes et al. 63 and Lovisari et al. 130, respectively), and decrease by one/two orders of magnitude in the core/galactic regions. In agreement with analogous samples (Babyk et al. 7), most of the objects have Mtot,c∼2×1011M_{\rm tot,c}\sim 2\times 10^{11} - 2×1013​M⊙2\times 10^{13}\,M_{\odot} within r<∼r\mathrel{\mathchoice{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\displaystyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr<\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\textstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr<\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\scriptstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr<\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\scriptscriptstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr<\crcr\sim\crcr}}}} 0.15 R500R_{500} (see Humphrey et al. 105 for comparable Mtot,gM_{\rm tot,g}). Moreover, we retrieve a Mtot,c∝Yx,c0.40±0.03M_{\rm tot,c}\propto Y_{\rm x,c}^{0.40\pm 0.03} scaling which is consistent with that found by Babyk et al. [7] with slope 0.38±0.05{0.38\pm 0.05}.2424 24 We note that as our sample extends down to isolated/low-mass galaxies, our scaling relations show a larger departure from self-similarity than those solely including massive ETGs and clusters (e.g., Vikhlinin et al. 231; see also Appendix A). Additional permutations of the halo properties can be retrieved via the total mass-to-light ratios shown in Fig. 24.

Figure 8 shows the M∙−MtotM_{\bullet}-M_{\rm tot} correlations retrieved via our customary Bayesian analysis (§II.2), together with the 1- to 3-σ\sigma scatter bands. As expected, Mtot,500M_{\rm tot,500} is purely a reflection of the X-ray temperature via R500∝Tx,5001/2R_{500}\propto T_{\rm x,500}^{1/2} (§II.1.2), thus preserving the small scatter of M∙−TxM_{\bullet}-T_{\rm x}. On the other hand, the correlation between M∙M_{\bullet} versus total mass within the core and galactic scale shows a significant intrinsic scatter, which is comparable to that of the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} and larger than that of most gas scalings. In particular, compared with the gas mass relation (§III.2.3), adding the DM component does not improve the mean corr coefficient and induces it to drop to a lower level. Under our assumptions, these results suggest that the plasma halos, and related baryonic properties, may play a more central role than the sole gravitational/DM potential in growing SMBHs. A positive correlation with MtotM_{\rm tot} is nevertheless established because hotter plasma halos are created in larger potential wells, as they get shock heated during the primordial halo formation. While a correlation cannot probe causation, we devote §IV to testing the BH mass growth via either gas accretion or mergers (which purely increase the gravitational potential), finding that the latter channel is sub-dominant over most of the cosmic time (§IV.1.4).

DM halos still represent a reasonable, useful proxy to predict the central SMBH mass. The correlation slopes are mildly superlinear, β≃1.2\beta\simeq 1.2 - 1.4 (with outliers becoming more frequent at the high-mass end). Such simple total mass scalings can be used by large-scale cosmological simulations (including both LTGs and ETGs) and semi-analytic models (SAMs) to either test their results or calibrate the subgrid parameters on the M∙−MtotM_{\bullet}-M_{\rm tot} (instead of the more complex stellar scalings; §IV.3). Another potential application is the inclusion of the AGN feedback power modeled directly from the DM mass; the latter is one of the best resolved and convergent properties in cosmological simulations (Sembolini et al. 196).

Interestingly, equating the total BH feedback energy E∙=η​M∙​c2E_{\bullet}=\eta M_{\bullet}c^{2} (§III.2.4) to the DM gravitational binding energy ∼\sim Mtot​ϕ≃Mtot​[3​kb​Tx/(μ​mp)]M_{\rm tot}\phi\simeq M_{\rm tot}[3\,k_{\rm b}T_{\rm x}/(\mu m_{\rm p})] ameliorates the above superlinear scaling into a quasi-linear mass scaling with β∼0.8\beta\sim 0.8 - 0.9 (outskirt to galactic scale; not shown). The retrieved BH mass (normalization) is similar to the observed one at the galactic scale, but is overestimated for the outer regions. In other words, M∙∼Mtot,g​ϕ/(η​c2)M_{\bullet}\sim M_{\rm tot,g}\phi/(\eta c^{2}) is a better proxy for BH mass than purely Mtot,gM_{\rm tot,g}.

III.2.6 Gas fraction

Now that we have MtotM_{\rm tot}, it is possible to analyze the gas fraction, which is the ratio between the gas mass and total mass, within the three enclosed radii, fgas=Mgas/Mtotf_{\rm gas}=M_{\rm gas}/M_{\rm tot}. Figure 9 shows that the inclusion of total mass weakens the likely more fundamental correlation with MgasM_{\rm gas}. The core region (where radiative cooling plays a key role) still preserves a low intrinsic scatter (≈\approx 0.250.25), with the two enclosing regions showing 35% larger ϵ\epsilon. We note that the propagated errors have now become substantial, given that fgasf_{\rm gas} is a highly composite variable. Remarkably, the slope is consistent with unity (considering 1-σ\sigma uncertainty), which allows for a straightforward linear-space conversion between gas fractions and BH masses.

Overall, it is evident that larger BHs prefer to grow in halos which host larger amount – both in absolute and relative sense – of diffuse gas, despite this being only a small fraction of the whole matter budget. Indeed, the retrieved core gas fraction for galaxies/groups hosting a few 109​M⊙10^{9}\,M_{\odot} BHs is a few percent (consistent with Sun et al. 212, Babyk et al. 7). Such fractions tend to approach the cosmic baryon fraction (∼\sim 0.1) when we consider the R500R_{\rm 500} of the cluster halo and the most massive BCGs (e.g., NGC 4889, NGC 3842; see also Eckert et al. 49). In this regime, feedback processes cannot easily evacuate the gas mass due to the large binding energy (Gaspari et al. 78). Conversely, the inner galactic/CGM region (strongly affected by AGN and stellar feedback) show values below the percent level (e.g., as found by Humphrey et al. 104, Humphrey et al. 105), in particular for isolated galaxies, thus requiring deeper and more challenging observations.

Moving forward, it will be crucial to obtain observations via X-ray telescopes with significantly improved sensitivity and resolution, for both imaging and spectroscopy, to test the faintest hot halos at the low-mass end and thus extending the sample to more late-type objects. A series of dedicated X-ray missions with such characteristics will operate in the upcoming decade, such as eROSITA, XRISM, Athena, and possibly AXIS and Lynx (see §IV.4 for more details on the future developments).

III.3. Multivariate correlations

A further key investigation angle that is worth dissecting is the Bayesian multivariate correlation analysis (§II.2) of the fundamental X-ray/optical variables. We limit the analysis here to a three-dimensional (3D) space, i.e., a correlation plane (with thickness given by ϵ\epsilon) with some inclination and position angle. In principle, higher-dimensional hyperplanes can be explored; however, the free parameters also increase substantially, thus diminishing the physical and predicting value of the fitting. This is also why the univariate correlations on the composite variables are in general preferred, given that the composite variables are set by physical intuition, rather than by a statistical random parameter search.

While the Bayesian prior/posterior procedure and MCMC analysis is essentially identical, an important difference with the univariate fitting is that, with mlinmix (Eq. 8), we are carrying out a dual partial (conditional) correlation analysis, implying that we will retrieve two partial correlation coefficients (related to X1X_{1} via the control variable X2X_{2}, and vice versa). Before dissecting the multivariate relations with BH mass, it is essential to first analyze the ‘fundamental’ planes in the optical and X-ray bands, in order to understand the major differences between the stellar and hot halos, and in which kind of environment the SMBHs reside and grow. Such planes are also crucial probes for competing evolution models of galaxies, groups, and clusters of galaxies.

III.3.1 Optical/stellar fundamental plane (oFP)

A key motivation to analyze multivariate correlations resides in the virial theorem (VT): a stationary system of particles bound by gravity is expected to have an average kinetic energy 𝒯\mathcal{T} directly related to the average gravitational potential energy UU such that

2​⟨𝒯⟩=−⟨U⟩.2\langle\mathcal{T}\rangle=-\langle U\rangle. (16)

For a virialized stellar system with σe,tot2=3​σe2\sigma_{\rm e,tot}^{2}=3\sigma_{\rm e}^{2}, we can write

σe2=κ3​G​M∗(<Re)Re∝LKRe,\sigma_{\rm e}^{2}=\frac{\kappa}{3}\,\frac{GM_{\ast}(<R_{\rm e})}{R_{\rm e}}\propto\frac{L_{K}}{R_{\rm e}}, (17)

where κ/3≈0.1\kappa/3\approx 0.1 - 0.32525 25 The normalization factor of the potential energy is tied to the detailed geometry of the particle spatial distribution; e.g., for a sphere with uniform density, κ=3/5\kappa=3/5. is a structural parameter and the second conversion mainly depends on the stellar mass-to-light ratio M∗/LKM_{\ast}/L_{K} (note that within ReR_{\rm e} the stellar mass dominates over the other mass components). It is important to note that the optical observables are only proxies for the intrinsic VT properties; the existence of an optical fundamental plane (oFP) among galaxies requires also significant (structural and dynamical) homology and tight M∗/LKM_{\ast}/L_{K} (e.g., Ciotti 34 and refs. within).

Figure 10 shows the edge-on view of the best-fit plane correlating (in logarithmic space) the three key stellar observables σe2−LK−Re\sigma_{\rm e}^{2}-L_{K}-R_{\rm e}. Since the virial theorem is centrally important, in this section we will adopt the velocity variance instead of the velocity dispersion. Notice that the plot abscissa implies a rotation about the YY axis, given by the two non-zero slopes. As is customary, the error bars are obtained by propagating the single errors weighted by β1\beta_{1} and β2\beta_{2}. The top-left inset lists the mean and standard deviation of all the posterior distributions of the Bayesian mlinmix analysis (Eq. 8).

Two are the key results. First, the measured multivariate optical properties are consistent with the VT prediction of a plane, as both β1\beta_{1} and β2\beta_{2} slopes have identical value but opposite signs. Second, the intrinsic scatter is very small (ϵ≃0.1\epsilon\simeq 0.1 dex). If we consider only the univariate correlations, the scatter increases up to 3×3\times and the corr coefficient decreases to the weak regime (as for the size versus velocity variance; Fig. 24); some of these univariate scalings indeed represent highly inclined projections of the best-fit oFP. In more detail, the multivariate result indicates that, over our whole sample, the virial relation σe2∝LK/Re\sigma_{\rm e}^{2}\propto L_{K}/R_{\rm e} holds tightly but with a mild tilt (1.4) in the slope, which departs from unity (below 2 standard deviations). The pcorr coefficients (0.9) further reflect the very strong positive/negative partial correlation related to LKL_{K} and ReR_{\rm e}, respectively. On the other hand, propagated error bars can reach relatively large uncertainty for lower mass galaxies.

The thin oFP is a well-known property, in particular for ETGs (e.g., Djorgovski & Davis 42, Dressler et al. 45). The tilt in the observed plane can mainly be attributed to the dependence of the stellar mass-to-light ratio on the velocity dispersion, M∗/LK∝σe0.3−0.4M_{\ast}/L_{K}\propto\sigma_{\rm e}^{0.3-0.4} (Kormendy & Ho 117). Further minor variations are due to DM, non-homology, and projection effects (cf. van den Bosch 250). Applying our stellar mass-to-light conversion (Eq. 1), we find a univariate correlation σe2=(0.20±0.02)​(G​M∗/Re)1.16±0.11\sigma_{\rm e}^{2}=(0.20\pm 0.02)\,(GM_{\ast}/R_{\rm e})^{1.16\pm 0.11}, which is close to Eq. 17 with κ∼3/5\kappa\sim 3/5.

Overall, the optical scalings can be filtered down to a single key variable, σe2\sigma_{\rm e}^{2}, or its virial analog LK/ReL_{K}/R_{\rm e}. Using MbulgeM_{\rm bulge} instead of LKL_{K} would show similar results (Fig. 26), although with significantly larger scatter due to the larger presence of disk-dominated galaxies at the low-mass end. In Appendix A, we include additional variants of the oFP, which may be of interest for other observational and theoretical studies.

III.3.2 X-ray/plasma fundamental plane (xFP)

We now dissect the X-ray fundamental plane (xFP) of hot halos, testing if the virial relation manifests so evidently in the plasma atmosphere too. This plane should not be confused with the AGN X-ray fundamental plane (Merloni et al. 147), which focuses on the nuclear X-ray luminosity of the central point source, instead of the ISM/IGrM/ICM LxL_{\rm x} and TxT_{\rm x}. The analog of the virial relation (Eq. 17) for a thermal plasma can be retrieved by using the specific thermal energy for the average kinetic energy such that

cs,i2≡kb​Txμ​mp=κ3​G​Mtot(<Rx)Rx∝LxRx,c^{2}_{\rm s,i}\equiv\frac{k_{\rm b}T_{\rm x}}{\mu m_{\rm p}}=\frac{\kappa}{3}\,\frac{GM_{\rm tot}(<R_{\rm x})}{R_{\rm x}}\propto\frac{L_{\rm x}}{R_{\rm x}}, (18)

where the first term is the gas isothermal sound speed. Since X-ray halos cover more extended regions than the stellar ReR_{\rm e} (Fig. 24), the probed total mass is no longer dominated by the stellar component, but by the DM. Interestingly, the hydrostatic equilibrium equation (neglecting the non-thermal pressure support term) is

G​Mtot(<Rx)Rx=−cs,i2​(d​ln⁡ned​ln⁡r+d​ln⁡Txd​ln⁡r),\frac{GM_{\rm tot}(<R_{\rm x})}{R_{\rm x}}=-c^{2}_{\rm s,i}\left(\frac{d\ln n_{\rm e}}{d\ln r}+\frac{d\ln T_{\rm x}}{d\ln r}\right), (19)

which is akin to a virial relation with the normalization κ\kappa given by the gas density and temperature log slopes2626 26 Typical large-scale gradients observed in groups/clusters give reasonable consistency between Eq. 18 and 19 normalizations..

Figure 11 shows the edge-on view of the Tx−Lx−RxT_{\rm x}-L_{\rm x}-R_{\rm x} best-fit plane.
