As for the optical properties, introducing a multivariate fitting substantially reduces the intrinsic scatter, showing a notable ϵ≈0.1\epsilon\approx 0.1 dex for both the galactic (top) and macro-scale core region (middle panel). At variance with the oFP, the β1,2\beta_{1,2} slopes are significantly different and much shallower than for a VT relation. The β2\beta_{2} slope is also consistent with null (within 1-2 standard deviations), meaning that the multivariate correlation reduces to the simple Lx−TxL_{\rm x}-T_{\rm x} relation. If we inspect pcorr, the conditional correlation is strongest for LxL_{\rm x}, for both the galactic and macro scale. We note that this is different from the univariate, non-conditional analysis, which indicates that the characteristic radii positively correlate with LxL_{\rm x} or TxT_{\rm x} (corr ≈\approx 0.7 - 0.8, ϵ≈0.2\epsilon\approx 0.2 dex; e.g., Fig. 24). Adopting the intensity Ix=Lx/(4​π​Rx2)I_{\rm x}=L_{\rm x}/(4\pi R_{\rm x}^{2}) better equilibrates the pcorr coefficients and lowers the scatter (bottom panel).

The xFP deviates significantly from the simple virial expectation, Lx∝Tx​RxL_{\rm x}\propto T_{\rm x}\,R_{\rm x} (Eq. 18; also called ‘self-similarity’ in cluster studies, modulo the cooling function Lx∝Tx​Rx​ΛL_{\rm x}\propto T_{\rm x}\,R_{\rm x}\,\Lambda). While stars are strongly collisionless systems solely driven by gravitational effects, the plasma halos are complex systems shaped also by thermodynamical processes (e.g., radiative cooling and feedback heating) as well as hydrodynamical/collisional features (e.g., turbulence, shocks, Kelvin-Helmholtz and Rayleigh-Taylor instabilities). Indeed, on top of the virialization process within the DM halo, the hot halos continuously experience multiphase condensation and feedback heating (from both stars and AGN; e.g., Gaspari et al. 78, Gaspari et al. 80), which evacuate and induce circulation throughout the macro atmosphere. The evacuation process is particularly important to reduce the density and thus the X-ray emission (∝n2\propto n^{2}) in less bound objects, ultimately leading to Lx∝Tx4.5L_{\rm x}\propto T_{\rm x}^{4.5} (Fig. 24). This observed steep scaling is consistent with other studies extending the luminosity – temperature relation down to low-mass and satellite galaxies (Diehl & Statler 40, Kim & Fabbiano 111, Kim & Fabbiano 112, Goulding et al. 87, Babyk et al. 7).

We can investigate in more detail the main reason for the difference between the oFP and xFP. Is the characteristic radius scaling the main culprit? If we analyze the univariate Re−σe2R_{\rm e}-\sigma_{\rm e}^{2} (Fig. 24), the optical log slope is 0.6±0.10.6\pm 0.1, which is consistent with the X-ray slope of Rx,c−Tx,cR_{\rm x,c}-T_{\rm x,c} (0.7±0.10.7\pm 0.1). The culprit is mainly the major difference between the optical and X-ray mass-to-light ratios. The optical M∗/LKM_{\ast}/L_{K} shows only very minor variations as a function of optical ‘temperature’ (T∗∝σe2T_{\ast}\propto\sigma_{\rm e}^{2}), with a log slope ≈\approx 0.2 (Eq. 1). The observed2727 27 Assuming simple cluster self-similarity, the predicted X-ray mass-to-light ratio would be Mtot/Lx∝Tx−1/2M_{\rm tot}/L_{\rm x}\propto T_{\rm x}^{-1/2}. X-ray counterpart instead shows a steep anticorrelation with X-ray temperature, Mtot/Lx∝Tx−3M_{\rm tot}/L_{\rm x}\propto T_{\rm x}^{-3} (Fig. 24). There are crucial differences between the X-ray and stellar emission. First, while LKL_{K} is essentially the sum of many black-body spectra with a given stellar age and metallicity, LxL_{\rm x} is instead given by plasma collisional ionization processes (∝ne​ni​Λ​(Tx,Z)\propto n_{\rm e}\,n_{\rm i}\,\Lambda(T_{\rm x},Z); §III.2.1). In addition, the above-mentioned heating processes break self-similarity, introducing a steep dependency between fgasf_{\rm gas} and halo mass (which otherwise would remain constant; Fig. 9 and Sun 209). In sum, the observed fundamental planes are a composition of more than three VT variables, including a mass-to-light ratio, such as

LR∝T(M/L)∝T∗0.8​(stellar)|Tx4​(gas),\frac{L}{R}\propto\frac{T}{(M/L)}\propto T_{\ast}^{0.8}\ {\rm(stellar)}\ |\ T_{\rm x}^{4}\ {\rm(gas)}, (20)

i.e., while galaxies with larger stellar velocity dispersion emit less optical light relative to mass, hotter plasma halos emit increasingly more X-ray photons. Since the shallow X-ray radius scaling is swamped by the stronger (Mx/Lx)−Tx(M_{\rm x}/L_{\rm x})-T_{\rm x} correlation, the observed xFP tends to closely approach the Lx−TxL_{\rm x}-T_{\rm x} projection (Fig. 11). Aggravating the difference is the several times larger intrinsic scatter of the X-ray (Fig. 24) versus optical (∼\sim 0.1 dex) mass-to-light ratio, which can be interpreted as a form of non-homology.

Recently, Fujita et al. [65] showed a variant of the xFP for 20 massive clusters (Mtot,vir>∼1015​M⊙M_{\rm tot,vir}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\displaystyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr>\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\textstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr>\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\scriptstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr>\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\scriptscriptstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr>\crcr\sim\crcr}}}}10^{15}\,M_{\odot}; Tx,vir>∼8T_{\rm x,vir}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\displaystyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr>\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\textstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr>\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\scriptstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr>\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\scriptscriptstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr>\crcr\sim\crcr}}}}8 keV) by analyzing lensing masses. While their mass/temperature range is far beyond that of our sample, it is interesting to note that they also find a tight (0.05 dex) xFP, involving Tx−Rs−MsT_{\rm x}-R_{\rm s}-M_{\rm s} (where MsM_{\rm s} is the mass within the NFW scale radius RsR_{\rm s}; Eq. 14). The significant thinness of the xFP is analogous to that in our Fig. 11, albeit 2×2\times larger likely due to the inclusion of galactic X-ray halos. Their plane substantially deviates from the simple virial expectation too, although it is unfeasible to compare absolute values, given the different observables and more pronounced self-similarity break of low-mass systems via non-gravitational processes.

III.3.3 Black hole mass versus oFP

We are now able to test the role of the SMBH mass in relation to the oFP and xFP. Fig. 12 shows M∙M_{\bullet} versus at least two of the oFP variables, with the usual posterior results of the Bayesian mlinmix analysis. The top panel shows that the BH mass – luminosity – size in the optical band is essentially equivalent to the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation (Fig. 3; see also Beifiori et al. 14, van den Bosch 250). Both have scatter consistent within 1-σ\sigma. As for the oFP (§III.3.1), the stellar luminosity/size shows pcorr strongly correlated/anti-correlated, with β1,2\beta_{1,2} slopes being specular at a value of approximately ±3\pm 3. Indeed using the oFP, M∙∝(σe2)2.2∝[(LK/Re)1.4]2.2∝(LK/Re)3M_{\bullet}\propto(\sigma_{\rm e}^{2})^{2.2}\propto[(L_{K}/R_{\rm e})^{1.4}]^{2.2}\propto(L_{K}/R_{\rm e})^{3}, as retrieved here. Overall, given the tight correlation between the stellar velocity variance and LK/ReL_{K}/R_{\rm e}, we can on average convert from one to the other, making stellar ‘temperature’ the unique fundamental variable for the optical component.

The middle and bottom panels show instead the multivariate correlations between M∙M_{\bullet} and the other two combinations of optical variables. Given the always higher pcorr (0.8 vs. 0.4) and steeper β1>β2\beta_{1}>\beta_{2}, it is clear that the dominant variable is σe2\sigma_{\rm e}^{2}. However, compared with the LK/ReL_{K}/R_{\rm e} correlation, the scatter is reduced slightly, even below that of the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e}. The major improvement is in comparison with the univariate M∙−LKM_{\bullet}-L_{K} (Fig. 3), reducing its scatter by 30%. By using the bulge mass instead of LKL_{K}, similar results would apply (Fig. 26). Overall, this shows that the multivariate optical correlations can improve the scatter, although only by a mild amount, and yet not below the level of most X-ray correlations.

III.3.4 Black hole mass versus xFP

Figure 13 shows the BH mass as a function of two other fundamental X-ray properties, varying between luminosity, temperature, and size, for the core region (the galactic region leads to similar results; Fig. 27). In all cases, the scatter remains on an almost identical level compared with the X-ray univariate correlations. When the size is involved (top and bottom panels), the LxL_{\rm x} or TxT_{\rm x} always dominates the pcorr coefficient. Indeed, as discussed in §III.3.2, the xFP is mostly driven by Lx−TxL_{\rm x}-T_{\rm x} (and related plasma processes). The thinnest plane involving the SMBH mass is achieved with M∙−Tx−LxM_{\bullet}-T_{\rm x}-L_{\rm x} (middle panel). The intrinsic scatter is significantly below any other optical multivariate scaling (§III.3.3).

Looking at the slopes, temperature displays the largest values. A drawback of the multivariate fitting is that it tries to statistically optimize the parameters, regardless of a potential physical meaning (this becomes progressively more severe with increasing number of dimensions). For instance, the linear slopes retrieved for M∙−Tx,c−Lx,cM_{\bullet}-T_{\rm x,c}-L_{\rm x,c} are polar opposite, β1≃1.6\beta_{1}\simeq 1.6 and β2≃0.1\beta_{2}\simeq 0.1; combining Tx3/2​Lx1/10T_{\rm x}^{3/2}\,L_{\rm x}^{1/10} does not lead to any evident thermodynamic property. Inspecting all the univariate scalings as a function of temperature, the closer composite variables are fgas,cf_{\rm gas,c} and RcondR_{\rm cond} (§IV.1.2), which uncoincidentally are among the properties with the lowest scatter. On a similar note, the normalization values do not evidently relate to physical constants. By investigating the alternative M∙−Ix−TxM_{\bullet}-I_{\rm x}-T_{\rm x} scaling (not shown), we find again that temperature dominates the partial correlations, for all the considered regions.

Overall, the fact that β1≫β2\beta_{1}\gg\beta_{2} and pcorr1≫pcorr2{\rm pcorr_{1}\gg pcorr_{2}} implies that the X-ray univariate fitting is minimally sufficient and better physically motivated. The tightness and simplicity of the xFP suggest that we can adopt either TxT_{\rm x} or LxL_{\rm x} as the key driver for the black hole mass growth, in a more confident way than the optical counterparts. To better quantify the last statement, we show in Fig. 14 the multivariate scalings (for the core region) between the xFP and specular oFP variable. While these planes are not significantly tighter than the pure M∙−M_{\bullet}- xFP scalings, they are instructive in showing how, in all cases, the X-ray property has a much deeper link to the SMBH mass (pcorr1≫pcorr2{\rm pcorr_{1}\gg pcorr_{2}}), even when σe\sigma_{\rm e} is involved, which is the key driver of the oFP (middle panel). Nevertheless, while the univariate scalings (§III.1) lead to a minimal and tighter interpretation (from the statistical and physical point of view), the presented multivariate (pure or mixed) scalings are additional stringent tests for theoretical/numerical models, which need to be passed to achieve a full theory of co-evolving stars, diffuse gas, and SMBHs in galaxies and groups of galaxies.

IV. Discussion – Physical Interpretation

In §III, we focused on the observed statistical correlations and comparison between X-ray and optical properties, at face value. Here, we discuss potential physical interpretations, caveats, and future developments.

IV.1. Testing SMBH growth mechanisms

By now, it is clear that the X-ray gaseous atmospheres play some relevant role in the growth of SMBHs. The models concerning the feeding of SMBHs arising from macro-scale properties2828 28 Since we are not probing relations with the AGN luminosity and given that we are concerned with the integrated BH mass over long timescales, accretion models dealing with the micro-scale of a few 10 RSR_{\rm S} are beyond the scope of this work (see also §IV.1.2). can be grouped into two major categories, hot/smooth plasma accretion (§IV.1.1) versus cold/chaotic gas accretion (§IV.1.2), which show different correlations between M∙M_{\bullet} and X-ray properties. Binary SMBH mergers are a third viable growth channel, which we probe in §IV.1.4.

IV.1.1 Hot gas accretion

The majority of hot accretion models are directly (or indirectly) based on the seminal work led by Bondi [23]. In a spherically symmetric, steady, and adiabatic gaseous atmosphere, the equations of hydrodynamics reduce to a simple formula for the accretion rate onto the central compact object (as per classical Bondi 23):

M˙B=λ​ 4​π​(G​M∙)2​ρ∞cs,∞3,\dot{M}_{\rm B}=\lambda\,4\pi(GM_{\bullet})^{2}\frac{\rho_{\infty}}{c^{3}_{s,\infty}}, (21)

where λ⁡(γ)\lambda(\gamma) is a normalization factor of order unity (λ⁡(5/3)=1/4\lambda(5/3)=1/4), and with the gas density and adiabatic sound speed, cs2=γ​cs,i2=γ​kb​Tx/(μ​mp)c^{2}_{\rm s}=\gamma\,c^{2}_{\rm s,i}=\gamma k_{\rm b}T_{\rm x}/(\mu m_{\rm p}), taken at large radii from the accretor, r∞≫rB≡G​M∙/cs2r_{\infty}\gg r_{\rm B}\equiv GM_{\bullet}/c^{2}_{\rm s}. The first drawback of the Bondi rate is that, as absolute value, it produces a very low accretion rate. Even assuming a fully formed SMBH for a median 1 keV galaxy, then M˙B∼10−4​M⊙​yr−1\dot{M}_{\rm B}\sim 10^{-4}\,M_{\odot}\,{\rm yr^{-1}}, i.e., a maximal accretion for 10 Gyr would grow the BH only by 106​M⊙10^{6}\,M_{\odot}. The inclusion of additional physics breaking the steady-state assumption (e.g., turbulence), spherical geometry (e.g., rotation), or adiabaticity (e.g., non-thermal support via radiation or magnetic fields), each leads to a further suppressed Bondi rate by over 1 order of magnitude (Proga & Begelman 180, Park & Ricotti 167, Gaspari et al. 77, Gaspari et al. 79, Ciotti & Pellegrini 35). Similar low/suppressed values apply to analogous hot accretion models, such as ADAF (advection dominated accretion flow) and related variants (e.g., Narayan & Fabian 159). A key property characterizes all hot, single-phase models: in order to accrete, the flow has to overcome the large thermal pressure support of the hot halo that strongly counterbalances (with negative radial gradient) the gravitational pull of the SMBH, galaxy, and cluster core. Eq. 21 is thus a firm upper limit for hot gas accretion models.

The last term in Eq. 21 is the key dependency tied to the hot X-ray halo. Combining the plasma density and sound speed, it can be rewritten as a steep inverse function of plasma entropy:

M˙B=λ 4π(GM∙)2(μ​mp)5/2γ3/2Kx,∞−3/2,\dot{M}_{\rm B}=\lambda\,4\pi(GM_{\bullet})^{2}\,\frac{(\mu m_{\rm p})^{5/2}}{\gamma^{3/2}}\,K_{\rm x,\infty}^{-3/2}, (22)

where the X-ray plasma entropy (related to the thermodynamic entropy as S∝ln⁡KS\propto\ln K) is defined as

Kx≡kb​Txnγ−1=kb​Txn2/3.K_{\rm x}\equiv\frac{k_{\rm b}T_{\rm x}}{n^{\gamma-1}}=\frac{k_{\rm b}T_{\rm x}}{n^{2/3}}. (23)

Figure 15 shows the BH mass versus the gas scaling of the Bondi rate (i.e., the plasma entropy2929 29 The M∙2M_{\bullet}^{2} dependence is a trivial self-correlation, which is unrelated to the X-ray halo. Eq. 24 also shows the key role of entropy. for a non-relativistic gas with γ=5/3\gamma=5/3). It is evident that the SMBH mass does not correlate well with the plasma entropy (thus hot-mode accretion), adopting any radial bin. All the corr coefficients reside in the absent or weak regime, even within the 1-σ\sigma level. The scatter is one of the largest reported in this study, ϵ∼0.6\epsilon\sim 0.6 dex, which is 3×\times that of the tightest X-ray relations, essentially spanning the entire observed BH mass range within the 3-σ\sigma channel. Even for the galactic case with mild slope (top), the weak correlation is negative, meaning hotter halos accrete relatively less gas mass, as stifled by the plasma pressure support (conversely to cold models which condense more heavily in more massive halos; §IV.1.2).

We can further test whether the integrated Bondi rate is capable of growing an SMBH to the current level throughout the cosmic history of the galaxy, group, or cluster. Integrating Eq. 22 (nonlinear ODE), ∫t0tHM˙B​𝑑t\int^{t_{\rm H}}_{t_{0}}\dot{M}_{\rm B}\,dt, and adopting a decreasing entropy with redshift Kx​(t)=Kx,now​(t/tH)θK_{\rm x}(t)=K_{\rm x,now}(t/t_{\rm H})^{\theta}, yields

M∙,B​(tH)=M∙,01−M∙,0Kx,now−3/2A(tH1−3​θ/2−t01−3​θ/2),M_{\bullet,\rm{B}}(t_{\rm H})=\frac{M_{\bullet,0}}{1-M_{\bullet,0}\,K_{\rm x,now}^{-3/2}A\left(t_{\rm H}^{1-3\theta/2}-t_{0}^{1-3\theta/2}\right)}, (24)

with integration constant given by the following: A≡λ​4​π​G2​(μ​mp)5/2​tH3​θ/2/[γ3/2​(1−3​θ/2)]A\equiv\lambda 4\pi G^{2}(\mu m_{\rm p})^{5/2}\,t_{\rm H}^{3\theta/2}/[\gamma^{3/2}(1-3\theta/2)]. We note there is no duty cycle for hot-mode accretion, since the diffuse atmosphere can not be removed and accretion remains continuous. Fig. 16 shows the fractional increase of the BH mass given a typical high-zz seed of M∙,0=105​M⊙M_{\bullet,0}=10^{5}\,M_{\odot} and θ=4/3\theta=4/3 entropy evolution (Voit 232). Assuming as boundary condition the galactic scale (top panel), the BH grows only a tiny mass fraction during the cosmic evolution (tH−t0≃13t_{\rm H}-t_{0}\simeq 13 Gyr), and it would worsen by adopting the large-scale Rx,cR_{\rm x,c} and R500R_{500}. The bottom panel shows the extrapolation of the Bondi rate down to the inner rBr_{\rm B} of each galaxy (<100<100 pc) by using the average observed CC entropy profile (K∝r2/3K\propto r^{2/3}; Panagoulia et al. 166)3030 30 By using the non-CC profile, the entropy would remain flat in the core, with no variation in M˙B\dot{M}_{\rm B}.. Even under such a best-case scenario the fractional increase reaches 1% and decreases toward the (hotter) BCGs due to the entropy dependence.

Overall, all the above tests rule out (even adopting favorable parameter values) hot-mode accretion as the primary mechanism of SMBH growth. This is consistent with high-resolution hydrodynamical simulations finding hot accretion sub-dominant compared with cold accretion (e.g., Gaspari et al. 76, Gaspari et al. 77). Moreover, applying the macro AGN mechanical efficiency (η=10−3\eta=10^{-3}; §III.2.4), the driven kpc-scale jet/outflow power for our median system is Pmech=η​M˙B​c2∼1039P_{\rm mech}=\eta\dot{M}_{\rm B}c^{2}\sim 10^{39} erg s-1, several orders of magnitude below the core X-ray cooling luminosity. This implies an inefficient AGN feedback mechanism (see also McNamara et al. 145, Russell et al. 187), together with a low-variability behavior inconsistent with most of the observed (X-ray) AGN light curves (e.g., Peterson et al. 174, LaMassa et al. 121).

IV.1.2 Chaotic cold accretion (CCA)

We test now the other main BH feeding theory, chaotic cold accretion (CCA), i.e., the raining of warm optical filaments and cold molecular clouds condensing out of the X-ray atmosphere via nonlinear thermal instability (§I). CCA behaves in a different manner from the above hot accretion models, displaying two distinct properties. First, the accretion rates can be boosted intermittently up to several orders of magnitude compared with the Bondi rate, given the recurrent chaotic inelastic collisions between the cold and warm clouds or filaments. Second, CCA displays large variability, with power spectral density described by a flicker noise, as shown by other natural chaotic and fractal processes, including AGN, quasars, meteorological data, and semiconductors (cf. Gaspari et al. 80). Moreover, this duty cycle is more frequent toward low-mass systems. In CCA-driven BH growth, the feeding and feedback processes are closely intertwined. While the rain recurrently triggers the AGN down at the horizon scale3131 31 Once CCA funnels the clouds within ∼\sim 20 Schwarzschild radii (rS≡2​G​M∙/c2r_{\rm S}\equiv 2\,GM_{\bullet}/c^{2}; Gaspari et al. 77), the Maxwell and Reynolds stresses generated via MRI turbulence in the inner torus induce the gas to radially accrete within ∼\sim10 orbital periods (Sa̧dowski & Gaspari 192, Jiang et al. 107), i.e., 10×2​π​[(20​rS)3/G​M∙]1/2∼10\times 2\pi[(20\,r_{\rm S})^{3}/GM_{\bullet}]^{1/2}\sim 2 yr (for M∙=109​M⊙M_{\bullet}=10^{9}\,M_{\odot}), which is negligible compared with the macro-scale plasma halo timescales. (Sa̧dowski & Gaspari 192), the AGN feedback quickly responds by injecting back a substantial amount of energy in the form of massive outflows and jets, which deposit their energy at the macro scale, in a gentle self-regulated feedback loop (e.g., Gaspari et al. 75, Gaspari et al. 76, Li & Bryan 126, Barai et al. 9, Yang & Reynolds 245, Yang & Reynolds 244, Yang et al. 246). Such mechanical AGN feedback, on the one hand quenches cooling flows, on the other hand induces over the long term an irreducible level of subsonic turbulence that shapes the halo weather (Lau et al. 125, Hitomi Collaboration 96, Simionescu et al. 203).

While expensive hydrodynamical simulations are required to track the detailed chaotic process (e.g., Gaspari et al. 77, Prasad et al. 179), analytic predictions can be retrieved from the macro-scale properties (Gaspari & Sa̧dowski 71). CCA is tightly linked to the cooling rate of the X-ray plasma:

M˙cool=q​μ​mp(3/2)​kb​LxTx,\dot{M}_{\rm cool}=\frac{q\,\mu m_{\rm p}}{(3/2)\,k_{\rm b}}\frac{L_{\rm x}}{T_{\rm x}}, (25)

where q≈10%q\approx 10\% is the evidence that most pure cooling flows are significantly quenched via AGN feedback (Peterson & Fabian 173, McNamara & Nulsen 144, Gaspari et al. 76). Since Lx/Tx∝t−1L_{\rm x}/T_{\rm x}\propto t^{-1} (Maughan et al. 135) and accounting for the CCA variability, the integral of Eq. 25 over cosmic time (tH−t0≃13t_{\rm H}-t_{0}\simeq 13 Gyr) leads to

M∙,cca​(tH)≃[M˙cool,now​tH​ln⁡(tH/t0)]​νccaν~cca,M_{\rm\bullet,cca}(t_{\rm H})\simeq\left[\dot{M}_{\rm cool,now}\,t_{\rm H}\ln({t_{\rm H}}/{t_{0}})\right]\frac{\nu_{\rm cca}}{\tilde{\nu}_{\rm cca}}, (26)

where the last term is related to the CCA rain active cycle, with a characteristic frequency given by the turbulent eddy turnover frequency (Gaspari et al. 81), νcca=(2​π​r2/3​L1/3/σv,L)−1\nu_{\rm cca}=(2\pi r^{2/3}L^{\rm 1/3}/\sigma_{v,L})^{-1}.3232 32 We note that for r>Lr>L, the eddy time reduces to ∝L/σv,L\propto L/\sigma_{v,L}, since the injection scale is the maximum driving scale. Indeed, turbulence is the key physics enabling the generation of significant overdensities in the stratified hot halo, which then nonlinearly condense in multiphase filaments and clouds. By using the ensemble warm-gas single spectra for 72 galaxies in groups and clusters, the above authors show that the (3D) turbulent velocity dispersion is contained in a fairly narrow range, σv,L≈240±30\sigma_{v,L}\approx 240\pm 30 km s-1, with a minor halo scaling ∝(Tx/ 2​keV)1/3\propto(T_{\rm x}/\,{\rm 2\,keV})^{1/3}. The injection scale LL is related to the AGN feedback influence region and can be retrieved from the observed size and distance covered by the pair of inflated AGN bubbles, scaling as L≈10​kpc​(Tx/1​keV)2L\approx{\rm 10\,kpc}\,(T_{\rm x}/{\rm 1\,keV})^{2} (Shin et al. 200) and reaching up to 200 kpc for massive clusters (e.g., MS 0735.6+7421). Further, the frequency of the CCA rain increases from massive clusters to low-mass galaxies due to the relatively stronger radiative cooling (Gaspari et al. 73, Gaspari et al. 75, Sharma et al. 199, Prasad et al. 178). While for low-mass systems the AGN feeding/feedback events are so frequent to be nearly continuous, massive clusters experience longer duty cycles, with powerful AGN outbursts (up to 104510^{45} erg s-1) followed by quiescent periods of a few 100 Myr. The last term in Eq. 26 models such CCA duty cycle, with normalization ν~cca\tilde{\nu}_{\rm cca} taken as the eddy frequency at the low-mass end of the halo distribution (ν~cca≈0.05\tilde{\nu}_{\rm cca}\approx 0.05 Myr-1). The retrieved median CCA frequency (with 1 RMS) over the whole sample is log⁡νcca/Myr−1≃−2.1±0.5\log\nu_{\rm cca}/{\rm Myr^{-1}}\simeq-2.1\pm 0.5.

The tight correlation between BH mass and X-ray luminosity (Fig. 2) already implies an important connection with the plasma cooling (and thus CCA), since its rate M˙cool\dot{M}_{\rm cool} is a strong function of LxL_{\rm x}. At variance with hot-mode accretion models (§IV.1.1), the CCA driven accretion rate is capable of generating SMBHs, and even UMBHs, over the whole Hubble time. Indeed, for a typical ETG cooling rate of 0.1 - 1 M⊙M_{\odot} yr-1, steady feeding would imply BHs with M∙∼M_{\bullet}\sim 10910^{9} - 1010​M⊙10^{10}\,M_{\odot}. While in hot accretion models the hotter the halo the lower the accretion rate, in CCA hotter – thus more luminous – halos drive stronger radiative emissivity and condensation. Similarly, the tight correlations found for M∙−MgasM_{\bullet}-M_{\rm gas} (Fig. 6) and M∙−fgasM_{\bullet}-f_{\rm gas} (Fig. 9), particularly in the core region (ϵ≃0.25\epsilon\simeq 0.25), support the key role of the gas mass in feeding the BH. On the other hand, the fact that M∙−LxM_{\bullet}-L_{\rm x} deviates from a pure linear scaling (β∼1/2\beta\sim 1/2) rules out cold accretion models that are perennially turned on over the entire mass range. Indeed, for massive clusters, such a model would generate UMBHs with masses in excess of 1011​M⊙10^{11}\,M_{\odot} during the Hubble time. The intrinsic chaotic variability of CCA, with retrieved lower frequency toward more luminous/extended halos, makes it a compelling model to solve such a hurdle.

Fig. 17 shows the quantitative CCA-driven BH mass growth computed via Eq. 26 and the X-ray properties of our sample. The best-consistent region to extract the CCA variables (as the cooling rate) is the core region (∼\sim0.1 R500R_{\rm 500}; middle panel). For the core region, the observed and predicted BH masses match in a linear way within 1-σ\sigma (β≃0.98\beta\simeq 0.98), covering the full range of detected masses from 3×107​M⊙3\times 10^{7}\,M_{\odot} to 1010​M⊙10^{10}\,M_{\odot}. The intrinsic scatter is the lowest among the three regions and tight (ϵ≃0.30\epsilon\simeq 0.30), with the correlation coefficient in the very strong regime (corr ≃\simeq 0.9). The galactic region instead shows a superlinear slope (top), since the M∙M_{\bullet} at the high-mass end are underestimated; the correlation is also weaker, displaying 30% larger scatter. Conversely, using the outskirt properties (bottom) leads to an overestimate of the BH masses in BCGs, inducing a too shallow slope; however, the correlation is still in the strong regime. Overall, the X-ray cooling rate initiating from the halo core region and then feeding the central BH appears to be the optimal predictor for the long-term3333 33 The instantaneous accretion rates in one cycle can be quickly estimated via LxL_{\rm x}; the total BH mass requires the integrated cooling rate, which is essentially the raining mass through several cycles. BH growth. This is further consistent with the core region correlating with the drop in temperature that differentiates CC versus non-CC systems (Vikhlinin et al. 230, Ghirardini et al. 84). It is also worth noting that the CCA average Eddington ratio is log⁡M˙∙,cca,c/M˙Edd=−2.7±0.4\log\dot{M}_{\rm\bullet,cca,c}/\dot{M}_{\rm Edd}=-2.7\pm 0.4, i.e., significantly sub-Eddington at the present time (but expected to slowly increase at higher zz; e.g., to −2-2 at z∼2z\sim 2), as found by X-ray AGN surveys (e.g., Aird et al. 2).

Another key property that is worth testing is the CCA condensation radius, RcondR_{\rm cond}. While significant X-ray cooling initiates in the core, the inner region where the condensed ionized (Hα\alpha+[NII]) filaments and molecular (CO) clouds end up precipitating is given by RcondR_{\rm cond}, the radius at which the eddy time (teddy=νcca−1t_{\rm eddy}=\nu_{\rm cca}^{-1}) and cooling time tcool≃3​kb​Tx/(ne​Λ)t_{\rm cool}\simeq 3\,k_{\rm b}T_{\rm x}/(n_{\rm e}\Lambda) become comparable, C≡tcool/teddy=1C\equiv t_{\rm cool}/t_{\rm eddy}=1 (Gaspari et al. 81). Given the electron density profile, ne​(r)=ne,c​(r/Rx,c)−an_{\rm e}(r)=n_{\rm e,c}\,(r/R_{\rm x,c})^{-a} (with median a≃1.6a\simeq 1.6 found in §III.2.1; see also Hogan et al. 99, Babyk et al. 7), a CC-ratio of unity translates into

Rcond=(32​π​kb​TxΛ​ne,c​Rx,ca​σvL1/3)32−3​a.R_{\rm cond}=\left(\frac{3}{2\pi}\frac{k_{\rm b}T_{\rm x}}{\Lambda\,n_{\rm e,c}\,R_{\rm x,c}^{a}}\frac{\sigma_{v}}{L^{1/3}}\right)^{\frac{3}{2-3a}}. (27)

Adopting the core properties, the M∙−RcondM_{\bullet}-R_{\rm cond} scaling shown in Fig. 18 (top) displays a tight correlation and linear slope (ϵ≃0.32\epsilon\simeq 0.32 and β≃0.98\beta\simeq 0.98) with corr coefficient in the very strong regime. This corroborates the above result (Fig. 17) that the growth of SMBHs is tightly linked to the CCA physics and related multiphase rain occurring in galaxies, groups, and clusters (see also Voit et al. 234, Voit et al. 235, Soker 205, Voit 233). In terms of normalization, ETGs in groups have Rcond∼0.6R_{\rm cond}\sim 0.6 - 6 kpc, while typical BCGs have Rcond∼7R_{\rm cond}\sim 7 - 40 kpc, which is in good agreement with the extent of Hα\alpha nebulae observed in low- to high-mass halos (McDonald et al. 139, McDonald et al. 140, Werner et al. 240; NGC 5044/A1795 a notable group/cluster with nebular warm gas). Using instead the galactic/R500R_{500} variables (not shown) leads to an underestimate/overestimate of the nebular radius by ∼\sim1 dex; the correlation with M∙M_{\bullet} is also weaker, with 40% larger scatter, signaling that we are moving away from the main thermally unstable plasma source (the core region).

It is important to note that RcondR_{\rm cond} is a function of predominantly TxT_{\rm x} (log slope ∼\sim2), thus, the tight M∙−TxM_{\bullet}-T_{\rm x} correlation found in Fig. 1 may be thought of as a reflection of the residual condensed phase recurrently feeding the central BH. This correlation is also linked to the gravitational potential (or R500R_{\rm 500}/total mass): hotter halos have larger gas mass, and thus more vigorous precipitation; in other words, larger, hotter halos have a more extended raining region (the role of mergers, also affecting the potential, is tested in §IV.1.4). Conversely, the characteristic radius of Bondi/hot models (§IV.1.1) is rB∝Tx−1r_{\rm B}\propto T_{\rm x}^{-1}, i.e., anti-correlated with hotter halos, hence going against the observed positive trend with BH masses, as well as being disconnected from the group/cluster properties (given its size of a couple orders of magnitude smaller than RcondR_{\rm cond}).

We can further test whether the CCA theory can self-consistently predict the Lx−TxL_{\rm x}-T_{\rm x} scaling relation based on the CC-ratio criterion. As the CC-ratio becomes unity, this yields a characteristic electron number density

ne,cond=32​π​kb​TxΛ​σv,Lr2/3​L1/3.n_{\rm e,cond}=\frac{3}{2\pi}\frac{k_{\rm b}T_{\rm x}}{\Lambda}\frac{\sigma_{v,L}}{r^{2/3}L^{1/3}}. (28)

The X-ray luminosity can then be retrieved via the integral shown in Eq. 9, adopting ne,cond2n^{2}_{\rm e,cond} (Eq. 28) in the emission measure, thus yielding

Lx,cond=275​π​(kb​Tx)2Λ​σv,L2L2/3​Rcond5/3,L_{\rm x,cond}=\frac{27}{5\pi}\,\frac{(k_{\rm b}T_{\rm x})^{2}}{\Lambda}\frac{\sigma_{v,L}^{2}}{L^{2/3}}\,R_{\rm cond}^{5/3}, (29)

with σv,L\sigma_{v,L} and LL given by the observational scalings (as a function of TxT_{\rm x}) discussed after Eq. 25. Figure 18 (bottom) shows the CCA prediction, by using the above RcondR_{\rm cond} in Eq. 29, compared with the independently observed Lx,gL_{\rm x,g}, with the condensation radius typically being ±0.3\pm 0.3 dex from the galactic/CGM scale. The match with the observed X-ray luminosity is good, with both normalization and scaling reproduced up to ∼\sim 1042​erg​s−110^{42}\,{\rm erg\,s^{-1}}, above which the scatter increases due to RcondR_{\rm cond} exceeding the CGM region. By extrapolating the density profile, Eq. 28 and 29 may be further generalized and applied in observational or theoretical studies to interpret or model the thermodynamic properties of diffuse media at different radii in a (semi)analytic framework. Summarizing, the predictions of CCA in terms of both the hot halo properties and SMBH masses are well in agreement with the analyzed observational data.

IV.1.3 Stars

As introduced in §III, the tightness of the X-ray temperature/luminosity/gas mass scalings (ϵ∼0.2\epsilon\sim 0.2 - 0.3), compared with the optical correlations (ϵ∼0.4\epsilon\sim 0.4 - 0.5) is an indicator that the gaseous atmospheres play a key role in the co-evolution of SMBHs. Besides the above quantitative tests, first principles suggest the stellar component is not the main source of fueling. Once rapidly collapsed from the progenitor molecular cloud, stars become collisionless, with negligible dynamical friction to feed the BH (this drag force is proportional to the square of the moving object mass). While SMBHs can efficiently accrete the collisional gas (in particular via chaotic collisions), the stellar component represents the residual, unaccreted mass that is progressively stored in the galactic potential.

The stellar mass is still linked to the gas condensation (hence the M∙−MbulgeM_{\bullet}-M_{\rm bulge}), however, the link with the BH growth is progressively washed out during the recurrent CCA cycles. Taking the potential (∝σe2\propto\sigma_{\rm e}^{2} or LK/ReL_{K}/R_{\rm e}) as reference improves the BH mass optical correlations, since the potential is less affected by the baryonic physics. While the stellar component can be well described via the VT and homology (as proven by the oFP; §III.3.1), X-ray halos are primarily affected by thermo-hydrodynamical processes (as found via the xFP; §III.3.2), rather than solely experiencing a virialization in a gravitational potential. The above results (and cosmological simulations in §IV.1.4) point toward gas accretion and condensation as the dominant mechanism establishing the relations with TxT_{\rm x} and LxL_{\rm x}, instead of such scalings being a pure passive tracer of the total mass/DM (Bogdán et al. 22). Needless to say, the secondary connection with the potential will be always present to some degree, as it sets an upper dynamical limit to any gas accretion3434 34 For an isothermal sphere ρgas=fgas​σe2/(2​π​G​r2)\rho_{\rm gas}=f_{\rm gas}\,\sigma_{\rm e}^{2}/(2\pi Gr^{2}), the dynamical limit is given by M˙dyn=4​π​ρgas​r2​σe≈103​σe,3003​M⊙​yr−1\dot{M}_{\rm dyn}=4\pi\rho_{\rm gas}\,r^{2}\sigma_{\rm e}\approx 10^{3}\sigma_{\rm e,300}^{3}\,M_{\odot}\,{\rm yr^{-1}} for fgas=0.1f_{\rm gas}=0.1. The cooling rate is much lower than this, as the X-ray halo is not collapsing in freefall. Integration by a timescale ∝σe1.5\propto\sigma_{\rm e}^{1.5} would lead to the observed M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation (e.g., King 113)., as well as being linked to the hierarchical merger growth – the focus of the next section.

IV.1.4 SMBH mergers

Another potentially important channel for BH growth is the hierarchical merger build-up throughout the cosmological evolution of galaxies and clusters. Let us discuss first a simple statistical approach, and then the more detailed realistic cosmological simulation. In the concordance Λ\LambdaCDM universe, the first galaxies form after ∼\sim1 Gyr after the Big Bang and start to stochastically merge into large-scale structures, such as proto-groups and then proto-clusters. Beyond a scale of tens kpc, the hosted SMBHs slowly sink (in a few Gyr) toward the new, merged potential center via dynamical friction onto stars, until the SMBH pair forms a hard binary. At the parsec scale, 3-body scattering with nuclear stars leads to the ejection of the stellar bodies and shrinking of the binary orbit to the milliparsec scale, where gravitational-wave radiation drives the final coalescence of the two SMBHs (e.g., Begelman et al. 12).

It is thus expected that, in a hierarchical universe, SMBH masses and any halo property positively correlate, including those of the X-ray plasma (which is heated up via the virialization shock during the infall in the DM potential). However, the key differentiating point is how well they correlate, in terms of slope and scatter. Idealized SAMs (Peng 171, Jahnke & Macciò 106) show that, starting from an uncorrelated random distribution of seeded intermediate BHs, a sequence of mergers will naturally lead to a linear correlation (β=1\beta=1) between SMBH mass and bulge/total mass, being both the results of a large number of summation events, which are independent from any gas feeding/feedback physics. In this ‘central-limit-theorem’ (CLT)3535 35 We preserve the CLT nomenclature adopted in the astrophysics literature; however, a better term would be to refer to this effect as an attractor in the evolution of a stochastic process. view, the ensemble averaging ensures that the fractional dispersion in both coordinates should decrease with increasing halo mass as ∝N−1/2\propto N^{-1/2}, assuming a very large number of experienced mergers NN. Rule of thumb for ‘large’ statistical samples is at least N=30N=30, hence a relative drop of the scatter down to 1/30≃0.181/\sqrt{30}\simeq 0.18.

Fig. 3 shows that the M∙−MbulgeM_{\bullet}-M_{\rm bulge} has a slope below unity (β=0.90\beta=0.90); the dispersion (from the best fit) for the bottom/top half of the bulge masses is 0.39/0.46 dex, which is inconsistent with the CLT prediction of a decreasing scatter. Fig. 8 shows that the M∙−MtotM_{\bullet}-M_{\rm tot} has a slope above unity for all the three main regions (β=1.2\beta=1.2 - 1.4); moreover, the dispersion in the top half of the total masses within Rx,gR_{\rm x,g}, Rx,cR_{\rm x,c}, or R500R_{500} is in all cases 1.1×\times that in the bottom half, i.e., opposite to the CLT prediction. This is supported by the below-described cosmological simulations (see also Fig. 4 in Bassini et al. 11), which further show that starting from a purely random uncorrelated distribution at large redshift is unrealistic, invalidating the CLT assumption. Analogous non-decreasing dispersion applies to the M∙−MgasM_{\bullet}-M_{\rm gas} correlations, which also have slopes deviating below unity (β≈0.6\beta\approx 0.6). All these results suggest that, while mergers are part of the evolutionary process, they are likely not the overwhelming force in the build-up of the SMBH – X-ray halo scaling relations.

To better quantify the above finding in a more realistic setup, we use state-of-the-art cosmological hydrodynamical simulations with subgrid models for baryon astrophysics, including radiative cooling, star formation, metal enrichment, and stellar/AGN feedback, which well reproduce the observed properties of X-ray hot halos (Rasia et al. 183, Planelles et al. 177, Biffi et al. 18, Bassini et al. 11 for the simulation setup). Such Lagrangian (SPH) zoom-in simulations of 135 groups/clusters of galaxies (Mtot,500∼1013M_{\rm tot,500}\sim 10^{13} - 1015​M⊙10^{15}\,M_{\odot}) are particularly useful to track the evolution and merging of the SMBHs (∼\sim 6000)3636 36 Softening/merging length of the sink particles is ∼3​h−1\sim 3\,h^{-1} kpc. hosted by each galaxy, in a large and robust statistical sample. Moreover, the simulations include subgrid modeling for both hot and cold gas accretion, as well as ejective (quasar-mode) and maintenance (radio-mode) AGN feedback (Ragone-Figueroa et al. 182 for the numerical details). Fig. 19 shows the median growth of the SMBH masses (normalized to the final mass) for the central galaxies over the ∼\sim 14 Gyr cosmological evolution (black), involving a combination of (predominantly cold) gas accretion and BH mergers. The orange/green line indicates the contribution of mergers, separating them into major/minor events, defined as having a mass ratio above/below 1:4, respectively. The first key result is that mergers contribute a sub-dominant fraction of the growing M∙M_{\bullet} over most of the cosmic evolution; only in the last Gyr they start to catch up with the level of gas accretion. It is important to note that Fig. 19 shows the SMBHs solely grown in central galaxies, thus experiencing the largest amount of mergers. As shown below (Fig. 20), over 70% of the total BHs do not experience a major merger and are entirely driven by (cold) gas accretion. Indeed, even with no mergers, the seeded BHs (starting at ∼\sim 105​M⊙10^{5}\,M_{\odot}) evolve toward the Magorrian relation. Overall, gas accretion is the main channel of SMBH growth for most of the population and over the long-term evolution, even in the best-case merger scenario of massive BCGs.

The second key result from Fig. 19 is that infrequent major mergers dominate the BH growth, rather than frequent small sub-structure accretion. The low rate of major galaxy mergers (∼\sim0.03 - 0.5​Gyr−10.5\ {\rm Gyr^{-1}} for z∼0z\sim 0 - 3; see also Rodriguez-Gomez et al. 185) means that for each final massive galaxy we expect ∼\sim2 major events during its evolution. In a similar vein, Fig. 20 shows our simulated Magorrian relation at z=0z=0 (for the entire galaxies), with the number of major BH-BH mergers highlighted with different colors for each final object. The SMBHs with a final mass of ∼\sim 5×107,5×108,5×109​M⊙5\times 10^{7},5\times 10^{8},5\times 10^{9}\,M_{\odot} have on average experienced 0, 2, 4 total major mergers (along the full tree), respectively. If we weight each major merger by the fraction of mass contributed to the final SMBH mass, such NN values are roughly halved. These results shows that binary BH major mergers are rare events, hence breaking down the CLT requirement of a significantly large N>30N>30. Moreover, computing the scatter in the simulated Magorrian relation for the sub-sample with N=0N=0, N<2N<2, or N>2N>2 leads to very similar dispersions of 0.2 dex, in contrast with the CLT expectation. The above combined results rule out hierarchical BH mergers and related CLT averaging as dominant drivers of the M∙M_{\bullet} versus (X-ray) halo scaling relations, making gas accretion the preferred – although not unique – channel. It is also important to point out that 75% of the simulated major mergers contain or bring a significant amount of gas very near the BH (‘wet’ mergers), meaning that they further enhance the gas accretion channel rather than the pure SMBH binary merging.

We note that another evolutionary formation scenario could be the full growth of SMBHs at very high redshift (z≫3z\gg 3). However, as shown by our cosmological hydrodynamical simulations (Fig. 19), over 99% of the BH mass is built at z<3z<3, since at very early cosmic times mergers are extremely rare and gas accretion is inefficient. Moreover, high-resolution simulations have still major hurdles in achieving the build-up of high-zz intermediate BHs with M∙<105​M⊙M_{\bullet}<10^{5}\,M_{\odot}, e.g., via direct gas collapse or supermassive/Pop III stars (e.g., Latif et al. 124, Luo et al. 131, Wise et al. 243), well before the SMBH regime. The handful of SMBHs observed at z>∼7z\mathrel{\mathchoice{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\displaystyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr>\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\textstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr>\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\scriptstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr>\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\scriptscriptstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr>\crcr\sim\crcr}}}}7 (e.g., Mortlock et al. 153) might thus represent the far tail of the random BH population; in addition, such measurements have highly uncertain masses due to the lack of direct dynamical measurements and large systematic errors in the modeling of the broad-line region. Instead of requiring all BHs to accrete at high-zz via unrealistically high gas accretion and/or mergers, the models and data suggest a gentler, long-term co-evolution of SMBHs (§IV.1.2) and host galaxies during the entire Hubble time.

IV.2. Relic galaxies, galactic coronae, environment, and morphology

Interesting astrophysical laboratories for testing the growth of SMBHs are compact relic galaxies, which appear to be the local analogs of high-redshift (z∼2z\sim 2) ‘red nuggets’, the progenitors of massive ETGs (e.g., Ferré-Mateu et al. 60, Werner et al. 241, Buote & Barth 28). These compact elliptical galaxies are thought to have formed 13 Gyr ago through early dissipative processes; however, at variance with other ETGs, they managed to randomly avoid the subsequent series of merging events, remaining fairly isolated until z=0z=0 with a passively evolving stellar population. They thus represent a direct probe for pure gas accretion models. Mrk 1216 and NGC 1277 are exemplary cases discovered in the local universe (D∼70D\sim 70 - 90 Mpc) with dynamically detected BH masses (Graham et al. 90, Walsh et al. 237). Both compact relic galaxies are among the major outliers in M∙−ReM_{\bullet}-R_{\rm e} and M∙−MbulgeM_{\bullet}-M_{\rm bulge} (up to 1 dex from the mean relations). Since they have not experienced the slow z<3z<3 non-dissipative phase that enlarges the stellar envelopes, their effective radii and bulge masses have remained relatively low, Re∼1R_{\rm e}\sim 1 - 33 kpc and Mbulge∼1011​M⊙M_{\rm bulge}\sim 10^{11}\;M_{\odot}, respectively (see Tab. 2). On the other hand, such compact galaxies host SMBHs with significant masses (M∙∼1M_{\bullet}\sim 1 - 5×109​M⊙5\times 10^{9}\,M_{\odot}); indeed, they possess galactic X-ray emitting atmospheres with Tx∼1T_{\rm x}\sim 1 keV. As they have been untouched by mergers for 13 Gyr, the only available source for accretion is the plasma atmosphere. Bondi hot-mode gas accretion drives too low accretion rates (§IV.1.1). Conversely, CCA mode is directly linked to the X-ray luminosity and can drive substantial accretion rates via the multiphase condensation of cold/warm clouds out of the persistent hot halo (§IV.1.2) from high to low zz, hence leading to the steady growth of BHs up to several 109​M⊙10^{9}\,M_{\odot} at the present time (regardless of the stellar component). Both relic galaxies consistently fit within ∼\sim1-σ\sigma of the BH mass versus Lx,gL_{\rm x,g} relation, indistinguishable from other normal ETGs in our sample.

Coronae are another class of dense X-ray atmospheres shrinked to ∼\sim1 - 5 kpc scale. They appear to be ubiquitous in ETGs (Sun et al. 211). Analogs of the above compact systems, they represent the irreducible hot X-ray atmosphere that co-evolves with the central SMBH; indeed, the relatively high gas density makes them survive stripping, evaporation, and AGN outflows. Thereby, even central ETGs in non-CC systems or satellites in poor environments can feed the SMBH via the condensation rain stimulated in the corona (for a very long time). Two examples of residual coronae are NGC 4889 and 3842 in the Coma and A1367 non-CC clusters, in which the galactic (corona) temperature seems to provide a better fit than Tx,cT_{\rm x,c}. We note that non-CC systems might have been CCs at higher zz, thus experiencing long periods of past macro rain.

Focusing on the environment, Fig. 21 (top panel) shows that satellite/isolated galaxies (gray) tend to have both low BH masses and low X-ray luminosity/temperature. Such galaxies are also correlated with late-type galaxies, such as S0s and spirals (with B/T<0.5B/T<0.5), mostly being in poor environments (Nm<10N_{\rm m}<10). While central galaxies sitting at the bottom of the group/cluster potential can feed from the macro plasma halo, satellite (and merging) galaxies are left to feed from the inner weather/corona, as they move at several 100 km​s−1{\rm km\,s^{-1}} relative to the external weather. If the stripping is, however, substantial, even the corona could be lost leading to undermassive BHs (perhaps the fate of dwarf galaxies as NGC 4486A with M∙<∼107​M⊙M_{\bullet}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\displaystyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr<\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\textstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr<\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\scriptstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr<\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\scriptscriptstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr<\crcr\sim\crcr}}}}10^{7}\,M_{\odot}). Similarly, isolated/field3737 37 Brightest field galaxies (BFGs; bold gray circles) can be considered analog of isolated galaxies, since the other field galaxies typically have a negligible contribution to the hot halo. galaxies are naturally starved of the large-scale gas reservoir. BCGs (red circles) host instead the largest BH masses up to 1010​M⊙10^{10}\,M_{\odot} of UMBHs, while BGGs (magenta) occupy the intermediate 109​M⊙10^{9}\,M_{\odot} SMBH locus (with NGC 1600 as an outlier, likely due to pure stochasticity). About 95% of such BCGs/BGGs are E-type galaxies (B/T≈1B/T\approx 1) and essentially all in rich environments (Nm∼10N_{\rm m}\sim 10 - 500). The more central the galaxy in a group/cluster potential, the more massive the X-ray halo and the larger the condensation radius (§IV.1.2), hence, with raining clouds and filaments that can be quickly (<∼100\mathrel{\mathchoice{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\displaystyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr<\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\textstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr<\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\scriptstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr<\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\scriptscriptstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr<\crcr\sim\crcr}}}}100 Myr) funneled toward the center of the group/cluster from larger BH distances. Conversely, as shown in §IV.1.4, group/cluster mergers are rare, with the formation of a binary SMBH via dynamical friction onto stars requiring several Gyr3838 38 The timescale of BH dynamical friction onto stars is (Combes 36) tdf∼2.5​Gyr​(vcirc/300​km​s−1)​(Re/5​kpc)2​(M∙/108​M⊙)t_{\rm df}\sim 2.5\,{\rm Gyr}\,(v_{\rm circ}/300\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}})(R_{\rm e}/{\rm 5\,kpc})^{2}(M_{\bullet}/10^{8}\,M_{\odot}). . Adopting instead the optical properties as σe\sigma_{\rm e} (bottom panel) shows that BCGs drive a major scatter and rough upward trend at the high end of the distribution (see also §III.1.2); thereby, the large-scale environment plays an important role in the evolution of SMBHs. In other words, the BH physics at the micro scale is substantially linked to the macro gaseous atmosphere thermodynamics, thus creating a unified symbiotic system (which may be referred to as ‘BH weather’) covering over ∼\sim10 orders of magnitude in spatial (and temporal) scale.

IV.3. Scaling relations as test/calibration for cosmological simulations

In §III, we presented a large set of scalings related to each of the thermodynamic quantities of hot halos, including the X-ray luminosity, temperature, electron density, pressure, thermal energy, and gas/total mass, both as univariate and multivariate correlations. Such a study is vital (i) to advance our observational constraints on the observable universe; (ii) to test/falsify models of BH accretion/growth; (iii) to carefully calibrate and check the predictive power of cosmological simulations. While the first two points have been amply dissected in the previous sections, let us focus on the last one.

Granted the relevant progresses in the past decade, state-of-the-art cosmological simulations still lack substantial resolution to implement all the baryonic physics in a self-consistent manner, thus having to rely on a simplified analytic approach known as ‘subgrid’ modeling (e.g., Sijacki et al. 201, Rasia et al. 183, Schaye et al. 193, Tremmel et al. 223, Weinberger et al. 239). This is particularly challenging for AGN feeding/feedback physics as it has to operate on scales spanning 10 dex. Most – if not all – subgrid models tend to calibrate the impact of AGN feedback and related SMBH growth on the optical scalings, in particular the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} or Magorrian relations. However, §III.1.2 - III.1.1 show that the optical scalings have significantly larger scatter than the X-ray halo properties and tend to steepen at the high-mass end due to UMBHs. As discussed in §IV.1.2, stars are indeed the final by-product of the top-down multiphase gas condensation that occurs throughout the cosmic time. Instead, the plasma halos are the primordial reservoir out of which the raining matter will feed recurrently the central SMBHs.

It is crucial to calibrate first the AGN feedback/feeding parameters of cosmological simulations on a few selected X-ray halo relations (e.g., M∙−TxM_{\bullet}-T_{\rm x}). The next step would be to check the predictions for all other thermodynamic properties (e.g., M∙−MgasM_{\bullet}-M_{\rm gas}) and/or stellar counterparts. The calibration should be as minimal as possible, in order to avoid overfitting. We note that calibrating first on M∙−MtotM_{\bullet}-M_{\rm tot} might lead to a large parameter-space uncertainty; as shown in §IV.1.4, the total (DM dominated) potential is likely a secondary element of the BH growth, while it is primary to model the hot gas physics first (e.g., galaxies without hot halos appear to show significant decorrelation from BH properties, regardless of DM mass). The dozen scaling relations presented in this paper should allow for multiple independent calibration tests to check the robustness of the subgrid model (see the recent work by Bassini et al. 11 for such an example). In parallel, subgrid prescriptions should gradually move toward physically-motivated – rather than fitting-oriented – models. E.g., a minimal subgrid approach based on a realistic AGN raining/outflow self-regulation is provided in Gaspari & Sa̧dowski [71]. Needless to say, the same scaling relations can be readily applied in purely SAMs of galaxy (e.g., Hirschmann et al. 95) and cluster (e.g., Flender et al. 62) formation.

IV.4. Caveats, selection effects, and future prospects

Before concluding, it is important to remark the limitations of the current work, selection effects, and expansions worth pursuing in future investigations.

The selection is first done in optical, as it is based on the available direct dynamical BH masses (§II). Since optical telescopes have to resolve the BH influence region, this limits our analysis to systems in the local universe (z<0.04z<0.04). Given the tight co-evolution of SMBHs and hot halos retrieved in simulations (e.g., Bassini et al. 11), we expect the retrieved M∙M_{\bullet} – X-ray halo correlations to hold at least up to z∼2z\sim 2 with similar scatter, albeit with steeper slope given the relatively slower growth of macro-scale cluster halos (Bassini et al. 11 find a M∙−TxM_{\bullet}-T_{\rm x} slope increase of 2×2\times from z=0z=0 to 2).

Regarding the X-ray selection, we only included direct BH masses with X-ray halo detections, except for a handful of contaminated systems (§II.1.2). The final sample of 85 systems includes a very diverse mix of morphological, dynamical, and environmental types (Tab. 2-3), hence we do not expect major biases in these directions. The vast majority of the galaxies with direct BH masses without X-ray detections are low-mass galaxies, which are expected to fall below a halo temperature of 0.2 keV and M∙<3×107​M⊙M_{\bullet}<3\times 10^{7}\,M_{\odot}, i.e., the IMBH regime. This is also related to Lx<1038L_{\rm x}<10^{38} erg s-1, which current X-ray instruments have severe difficulties in constraining. Extrapolating the M∙−TxM_{\bullet}-T_{\rm x}, these IMBHs should reside in the UV regime (e.g., NGC 2787 and NGC 7582 at 0.18 keV show already signs of being unconstrained in X-rays), which is not sufficiently covered by any current telescope. This IMBH regime corresponds to low-mass galaxies with M∗<5×109​M⊙M_{\ast}<5\times 10^{9}\,M_{\odot}. Bulgeless disk galaxies have been shown to start to deviate from the mean optical scalings (Kormendy & Ho 117), and might present a challenge for those involving hot halos too. Such departures can be due to the low binding energy of small halos and thus higher susceptibility to AGN feedback evacuation. Moreover, low-mass galaxies experience rotation as dominant physics, which changes the formation and frequency of the condensation rain (Gaspari et al. 79), reducing the accreted gas mass via the stronger centrifugal barrier (as a function of the turbulent Taylor number Tat≡vrot/σv{\rm Ta_{t}}\equiv v_{\rm rot}/\sigma_{v}, linked to B/TB/T; e.g., Juráňová et al. 108). Overall, given the above effects, we envision an increased scatter and steeper/lower slope/normalization in the correlations including such unprobed low-mass regime. Further, rapid rotation triggers different accretion mechanisms such as disk shearing and bar/ring instabilities (Hopkins & Quataert 100); it may be thus worthwhile to explore other correlations, as that between M∙M_{\bullet} and the spiral-arm pitch angle (Davis et al. 39).

Another relevant problem moving toward IMBHs and low-mass galaxies/halos is the fact that X-ray binaries (XBs) start to swamp the diffuse hot gas emission. As shown by the stacking of the ROSAT X-ray emission of over 250 000 galaxies (Anderson et al. 4; their Fig. 5), at log⁡M∗/M⊙<10.7\log M_{\ast}/M_{\odot}<10.7, XBs dominate the X-ray luminosity. Similarly, X-ray AGN/quasars with high Eddington ratio (>∼0.05\mathrel{\mathchoice{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\displaystyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr>\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\textstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr>\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\scriptstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr>\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\scriptscriptstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr>\crcr\sim\crcr}}}}0.05) can introduce significant uncertainty in the X-ray halo detection, especially in Seyfert galaxies (conspicuously contaminating AGN can even be hosted in BCG, as in NGC 1275). Active starbursts drive plasma energized via stellar winds and supernovae, thus creating a marked soft X-ray excess (LaMassa et al. 120; e.g., NGC 7582) and often require uncertain 2-TT models (the hotter component tied to the starburst/spiral arms, the cooler component to the diffuse gas; Li & Wang 127). Interestingly, for one of the closest dwarf galaxies M32 (NGC 0221; D≃0.8D\simeq 0.8 Mpc), it is possible to put a crude constraint on log⁡Lx/1044​erg​s−1≈−7.9±0.2\log L_{\rm x}/{\rm 10^{44}\,erg\,s^{-1}}\approx-7.9\pm 0.2 (Boroson et al. 26), which is consistent within 1-σ\sigma from the extrapolated mean M∙−Lx,gM_{\bullet}-L_{\rm x,g} (Fig. 2); however, such measurement remains tentative considering the 2 dex larger LxL_{\rm x} by XBs (plus ABs and CVs).

While the X-ray properties are in general a more robust indicator of the BH mass growth compared with the stellar properties, extreme events driving shocks can cause the hot halo to become overheated up to R500R_{500}. In particular, ongoing wet major mergers can drive strong shocks (Mach>10{\rm Mach>10}) over large regions of the group/cluster (e.g., Vazza et al. 229), thus temporarily biasing the halo TxT_{\rm x} toward larger values. Violent AGN jet cocoon shocks and hotspots lead to analogous bias (enhancing LxL_{\rm x} too via major density compressions), albeit being contained mostly in the CGM/core region. We have retained in our sample the large majority of such systems (e.g., NGC 5128, NGC 1316, NGC 7626, UGC 12064, NGC 1399), except for the dramatic case of 3C405 (Cygnus A), whose X-ray emission is fully dominated by the bipolar lobes driven via the 100 kpc FRII jets. All the above objects increase the scatter. To achieve tighter M∙M_{\bullet} – X-ray halo correlations, future studies may thus aim to mask the strong anisotropic merger/jet features (e.g., as done for NGC 3801) or to separate the shocked medium from the diffuse halo via a 2-TT fit analysis (e.g., as carried out for NGC 2110).

Given the above limitations, future investigations should be aimed to better probe the low-mass, disk (B/T≪0.3B/T\ll 0.3) regime, in terms of direct dynamical BH mass measurements (e.g., by using ALMA sub-arcsec resolution to detect circumnuclear molecular disks; Barth et al. 10), while moving toward the very soft X-ray (e.g., Athena) or UV emission regime (e.g., HST/COS). At the same time, the community should aim to expand the direct BH mass measurements in the BCGs of massive clusters with Tx,c>2T_{\rm x,c}>2 keV, of which there are only a handful available at the present. The very-high-end regime is important to fill: can the universe develop UMBHs with masses in excess of 20 billion M⊙M_{\odot} or will a saturation develop? Enlarging the cluster sample is also crucial to test whether the scatter of the (more uncertain) R500R_{500} scalings remains smaller than that of the optical scalings. In terms of evolution, we should aim to push BH mass detections at higher zz, understanding whether the presented M∙M_{\bullet} – X-ray scaling relations develop already with the formation of the first CC clusters (e.g., McDonald et al. 141).

Future X-ray observations – leveraging next-generation telescopes like Athena3939 39 https://www.the-athena-x-ray-observatory.eu (Nandra et al. 158, Ettori et al. 51), XRISM4040 40 https://heasarc.gsfc.nasa.gov/docs/xrism (Kitayama et al. 115), eROSITA4141 41 https://www.mpe.mpg.de/eROSITA (Merloni et al. 148), and possibly AXIS4242 42 http://axis.astro.umd.edu (Mushotzky et al. 155) and Lynx4343 43 https://www.lynxobservatory.com (Gaskin et al. 69) – should aim to improve the exposure, not only of hot halos in LTGs, but also in the outer regions of the host group and cluster (e.g., as carried out with the X-COP program; Eckert et al. 49). Expanding the sample toward isolated galaxies (Nm=1N_{\rm m}=1; e.g., NGC 7457) and compact relic galaxies is also crucial, albeit very challenging, requiring very deep X-ray observations (with exposure ≫300\gg 300 ks); however, such systems are excellent laboratories to test the differences with BCGs/BGGs and disentangle the gas accretion versus merger channel. Further, achieving a finer radial profiling of the hot halo properties for the whole sample would help to better elucidate the variation of the BH scaling relations over more homogeneous extraction radii. A more accurate determination of the X-ray half-light radius would also facilitate the comparison with ReR_{\rm e}, and better determine the virialization of hot halos in the multivariate xFP. Finally, direct detections of total masses (e.g., via lensing) and other gas mass properties as YszY_{\rm sz} (e.g., via CMB) would help to relax our derived properties assumptions and better probe the large scales, in particular at and beyond R500R_{500}.

V. Conclusions

We thoroughly probed the thermodynamical correlations between SMBHs and X-ray emitting plasma halos for 85 systems (Tab. 1), through a large literature search and Bayesian analysis approach (§III), as well as from a theoretical perspective testing different theories and mechanisms (§IV). We probed univariate and multivariate (FPs) correlations over three major radial extraction regions, galactic, group/cluster core, and outskirt regions (r∼r\sim 0.03, 0.15, 1.0 R500R_{500}), including a wide range of systems, spanning from massive galaxies to isolated S0s and spiral galaxies. The main results are as follows.

  • •

    We found key novel BH mass versus X-ray halo (univariate) correlations, first in terms of fundamental variables, with the tightest relation being the M∙−TxM_{\bullet}-T_{\rm x} (slope 2.1 - 2.7), followed by M∙−LxM_{\bullet}-L_{\rm x} (slope 0.4 - 0.5) The intrinsic scatter is significantly low, ϵ=0.2\epsilon=0.2 - 0.3 dex, in particular adopting the galactic/core region for the temperature/luminosity. The correlation coefficients are in the very strong regime (corr >∼0.9\mathrel{\mathchoice{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\displaystyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr>\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\textstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr>\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\scriptstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr>\crcr\sim\crcr}}}{\lower 2.5pt\vbox{\halign{$\mathsurround 0pt\scriptscriptstyle\hfil#\hfil$\cr>\crcr\sim\crcr}}}}0.9). X-ray halos are thus excellent indicators for SMBH masses hosted by diverse types of galaxies (BCGs/satellites or ETGs/LTGs) with luminosities spanning over 6 dex. On average, a 0.8 keV or 1041​erg​s−110^{41}\;{\rm erg\,s^{-1}} hot halo is expected to host an SMBH with 109​M⊙10^{9}\,M_{\odot}.

  • •

    We compared the X-ray/plasma scalings with the optical/stellar counterparts (M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e}, M∙−LKM_{\bullet}-L_{K}, Magorrian), finding that the stellar scalings have significantly larger scatter, ϵ≈0.4\epsilon\approx 0.4 - 0.5. This and the pairwise residual correlation analysis suggest a more fundamental role of gaseous halos in growing and tracing SMBHs. The UMBH regime is well fitted via the X-ray scalings (including the cluster/group halo), while it increases the scatter in the stellar scalings; indeed, unlike satellites and field/isolated galaxies, central BCGs/BGGs can efficiently feed from the macro plasma halo. A median 109​M⊙10^{9}\,M_{\odot} SMBH is hosted by galaxies with σe≈260​km​s−1\sigma_{\rm e}\approx 260\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}, LK≈4×1011​L⊙L_{K}\approx 4\times 10^{11}\,L_{\odot}, and Mbulge≈3×1011​M⊙M_{\rm bulge}\approx 3\times 10^{11}\,M_{\odot}.

  • •

    We presented new BH mass (univariate) correlations in terms of the composite/derived X-ray variables: M∙−MgasM_{\bullet}-M_{\rm gas} (slope 0.5 - 0.6) is among the tightest and strongest correlations (corr ∼\sim 0.9), in particular within the group/cluster core region, with half the scatter of the Magorrian; remarkably, a 109​M⊙10^{9}\,M_{\odot} SMBH is hosted by a hot halo with same Mgas,g≈109​M⊙M_{\rm gas,g}\approx 10^{9}\,M_{\odot}. M∙−PxM_{\bullet}-P_{\rm x} and M∙−neM_{\bullet}-n_{\rm e} have significantly larger scatter (especially in the galactic region), the latter approaching a quasi linear scaling. M∙−YxM_{\bullet}-Y_{\rm x} is instead stable (slope ≃1/2\simeq 1/2) and tight (ϵ≃0.3\epsilon\simeq 0.3) over all regions, and can be leveraged by SZ observations up to R500R_{500} (hot halos with Yx,c≈6×1058​ergY_{\rm x,c}\approx 6\times 10^{58}\,{\rm erg} typically host 109​M⊙10^{9}\,M_{\odot} SMBHs).

  • •

    Besides the trivial M∙−Mtot,500M_{\bullet}-M_{\rm tot,500} inherited from TxT_{\rm x}, the total mass MtotM_{\rm tot} is less correlated with BH mass than most gas relations, showing superlinear slopes (β≃1.2\beta\simeq 1.2 - 1.4) and significant scatter comparable to that of the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} (a better alternative is to use the binding energy M∙∝Mtot​ϕM_{\bullet}\propto M_{\rm tot}\phi). The M∙−fgasM_{\bullet}-f_{\rm gas} unveils a tighter connection with the BH mass (as for MgasM_{\rm gas}), establishing a linear relation (β≃1\beta\simeq 1) over all regions. Under our assumptions, this and above gas scalings suggest that M∙M_{\bullet} correlates better with X-ray halos rather than DM halos.

  • •

    The multivariate correlation analysis of the optical (oFP) and X-ray fundamental plane (xFP) shows that, while the stellar observables can be well described via the virial theorem (plus homology) in a multivariate fundamental plane (σe2∝LK/Re\sigma_{\rm e}^{2}\propto L_{K}/R_{\rm e}), X-ray halos are better described by the univariate scalings (e.g., Lx∝Tx4L_{\rm x}\propto T_{\rm x}^{4}), with major deviations from self-similarity and primarily driven by plasma physics, rather than a pure virialization. The main difference between the optical and X-ray component resides in the mass-to-light ratios (M∗/LK∝T∗0.2M_{\ast}/L_{K}\propto T_{\ast}^{0.2} vs. Mtot/Lx∝Tx−3M_{\rm tot}/L_{\rm x}\propto T_{\rm x}^{-3}).

  • •

    Given the existence of the oFP/xFP, multivariate correlations between M∙M_{\bullet} and (statistical) combinations of X-ray/optical properties leads to a minor scatter improvement; the above univariate correlations (especially involving TxT_{\rm x} and σe2\sigma_{\rm e}^{2}) are a better minimal interpretation of BH growth. The partial correlation analysis of the mixed X-ray and optical properties (e.g., M∙−Tx−σe2M_{\bullet}-T_{\rm x}-\sigma_{\rm e}^{2} and M∙−Lx−LKM_{\bullet}-L_{\rm x}-L_{K}) corroborates that hot halos are more tightly linked to M∙M_{\bullet} rather than the stellar component.

  • •

    We tested the three major channels for M∙M_{\bullet} growth: hot gas (Bondi-like) accretion, chaotic cold accretion (CCA), and mergers. Hot/smooth accretion models are rejected by the data being anti-correlated with plasma-halo properties and inducing too low feeding levels. Hierarchical binary BH mergers are sub-dominant during most of the cosmic time, with CLT predictions and assumptions inconsistent with our data and cosmological simulation; the latter shows that major mergers are rare and do not substantially decrease the scatter at the high-mass end. The X-ray scaling relations and simulations indicate a key role of CCA (with predictions consistent with the observed BH mass growth, halo dependence, and condensation radius), whose rain is induced by the cooling of the turbulent plasma halo (tied to LxL_{\rm x}/TxT_{\rm x} and MgasM_{\rm gas}) and balanced by the AGN feedback cycling through the Hubble time.

  • •

    Relic galaxies (descendant of high-zz red nuggets) and galactic coronae, both having sizes of a few kpc, are vital astrophysical laboratories to test the SMBH growth via purely gas accretion, since the former have been untouched by mergers for 13 Gyr and the latter can survive extreme or poor environments, thus enabling the recurrent inner feeding via gas condensation. On the other hand, galaxies at the center of rich environments (large NmN_{\rm m} or B/TB/T, and early types) can feed from the macro-scale rain forming UMBHs.

  • •

    The new X-ray halo correlations can be leveraged to calibrate and test large-scale cosmological simulations with AGN feeding/feedback subgrid schemes, as well as SAMs of galaxy and cluster formation. These can be now carried out from multiple angles not only in terms of LxL_{\rm x} and TxT_{\rm x} (plasma studies), but also via gas pressure/thermal energy (SZ studies), gas fractions (cosmological studies), and total/DM masses (lensing studies).

In sum, the BH physics at the micro scale is tightly linked to the macro gaseous atmosphere thermodynamics, thus creating a unique symbiotic system (which we refer to as ‘black hole weather’) spanning over ∼\sim10 orders of magnitude in space and time (as predicted by first-principle arguments; Gaspari & Sa̧dowski 71). This study highlights the importance of combining both observational analysis (and exquisite single studies produced in the literature) with a deep theoretical/numerical interpretation. We live exciting times for multiphase SMBH feeding/feedback observations and modeling, with new missions directly probing and discovering the multiphase halo rain and AGN outflows (Chandra, XMM, ALMA, MUSE, MUSTANG-2, LOFAR, SOFIA) and with next-generation telescopes that might be able to open new windows on multi-messenger processes related to SMBHs and gaseous halos (Athena, eROSITA, XRISM, EHT, JWST, SPT-3G, LSST, SKA, LISA). These programs will lead to order-of-magnitude leaps in sample size, sensitivity, and accuracy, and thus, in our understanding of BHs and their co-evolution with the host galaxies, groups and clusters of galaxies.

Appendix A A. Complementary scalings

We include here additional univariate and multivariate scalings complementary to the discussion in §III - IV. Such scalings can be useful for other studies that intend to probe and/or calibrate their parameters on a wider range of observational constraints. Being secondary and mentioned in the above sections, we do not dissect each scaling, although we provide insights in each caption. The interested reader can assess the quantitative properties of the correlations from the inset, listing the mean and standard deviations for all the posterior distributions (§II.2). Additional permutations of the scalings can be easily computed by combining the below correlations and/or those in Tab. 1.
